# Search Studio — full explanations

## Breadth First Search (week 2, Graph search · uninformed)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-bfs.html

Breadth First Search explores in rings: first everything one step from the start, then two steps, and so on. It finds the path with the fewest edges.

Definition: A state-space search problem has a start node S, a goal test, and a MoveGen function that lists the neighbours of a node. The search keeps two lists: OPEN (nodes generated but not yet expanded) and CLOSED (nodes already expanded). Each entry is a node pair (node, parent, value) so the path can be read back through parents. BFS treats OPEN as a queue: new children go to the back.

Pseudocode:

```
OPEN ← [(S, nil, 0)];  CLOSED ← [ ]
while OPEN not empty
    (N, parent, d) ← head(OPEN);  remove it
    if GoalTest(N): return the path via parent pointers
    CLOSED ← (N, parent, d) : CLOSED
    children ← MoveGen(N) minus nodes on OPEN or CLOSED
    OPEN ← OPEN ++ [(C, N, d+1) for C in children]     # append = queue
return failure
```

- nodes ≈ b^d: branching factor to the power of the goal depth. BFS must hold an entire level of the tree in OPEN: memory, not time, is its bottleneck.

Complete on finite graphs and optimal when every edge costs the same. Uses a lot of memory.

Complete: yes. Optimal: yes for unit costs. Time: O(b^d). Space: O(b^d).

- Trap: Optimal in number of edges, not in total cost when edge costs differ: on graph-weighted or graph-greedy-detour the fewest-edge path is not the cheapest.
- Trap: Compare with DFS on graph-dfs-deep: BFS returns the 3-edge path but must hold a whole level on OPEN.
- Trap: Children are added in MoveGen order (alphabetical here).

## Depth First Search (week 2, Graph search · uninformed)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-dfs.html

Depth First Search goes as deep as possible along one path before backing up. It needs little memory but can wander far from a nearby goal.

Definition: A state-space search problem has a start node S, a goal test, and a MoveGen function that lists the neighbours of a node. The search keeps two lists: OPEN (nodes generated but not yet expanded) and CLOSED (nodes already expanded). Each entry is a node pair (node, parent, value) so the path can be read back through parents. DFS treats OPEN as a stack: new children go to the front.

Pseudocode:

```
OPEN ← [(S, nil, 0)];  CLOSED ← [ ]
while OPEN not empty
    (N, parent, d) ← head(OPEN);  remove it
    if GoalTest(N): return the path
    CLOSED ← (N, parent, d) : CLOSED
    children ← MoveGen(N) minus nodes on OPEN or CLOSED
    OPEN ← [(C, N, d+1) for C in children] ++ OPEN     # prepend = stack
return failure
```

- space ≈ b · m: branching factor times maximum depth. Only the current path and the siblings along it are stored.

Memory-light, but neither optimal nor guaranteed to finish on infinite or very deep spaces.

Complete: finite graphs only. Optimal: no. Time: O(b^m). Space: O(b·m).

- Trap: DFS returns the first goal it dives into, not the shortest path: on example graph-dfs-deep it returns a 5-edge path S–A–C–D–E–G while BFS finds the 3-edge S–B–F–G.
- Trap: The path found depends heavily on MoveGen order: reverse the order of the neighbours and the other branch would be tried first.
- Trap: Do not confuse the order children are pushed with the order they are expanded.
- Trap: On an infinite or very deep graph DFS may never come back from one branch; the CLOSED list only protects it on finite graphs (**supplementary**: the course graphs here are all finite).

## Depth-Bounded DFS (week 2, Graph search · uninformed)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-dfs-bounded.html

Depth-bounded DFS is plain Depth First Search with a ceiling on depth. A node at the bound is tested but never expanded, so the search cannot dive forever down one branch.

Definition: OPEN is a stack of node pairs (N, parent, depth). The start node has depth 0 and a child has depth(parent)+1. When the node taken from OPEN has depth equal to the bound, it is goal-tested but no children are generated. If OPEN empties without reaching the goal, there is no goal within the bound (the search is incomplete: a deeper goal is not ruled out).

Pseudocode:

```
OPEN ← [(S, nil, 0)];  CLOSED ← [ ]
while OPEN not empty
    (N, parent, d) ← head(OPEN);  remove it
    if GoalTest(N): return the path
    CLOSED ← (N, parent, d) : CLOSED
    if d < depthBound:
        children ← MoveGen(N) minus nodes on OPEN or CLOSED
        OPEN ← [(C, N, d+1) for C in children] ++ OPEN     # stack
return failure   (no goal within the bound)
```

- depth(C) = depth(N) + 1: a child is one level deeper. Depth is what the bound limits.
- expand N only if depth(N) < bound: stop generating at the ceiling. This guarantees every branch has finite length, so the search terminates.

It is the building block of DFID: run it with bound 0, 1, 2, … to get the completeness of BFS with the memory of DFS. On its own it is incomplete, and the path it finds is not guaranteed to be shortest.

Complete: no (only if the goal is within the bound). Optimal: no. Time: O(b^bound). Space: O(b·bound).

- Trap: A bound that is too small fails even though a goal exists: failure only means no goal within the bound (graph-dfs-deep: bound 2 fails, bound 3 finds the goal at depth 3).
- Trap: Even a bound that is large enough can fail with a CLOSED list: a node first reached by a long route is closed at the bound and a later short route to it is skipped (graph-dfid-closed, bound 3 fails; DFID succeeds there because it reopens such nodes).
- Trap: A bound that is too large behaves like plain DFS and can find a long, winding path.
- Trap: The goal test applies to nodes at the bound too; only their expansion is skipped.

## Depth First Iterative Deepening (week 2, Graph search · uninformed)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-dfid.html

Depth First Iterative Deepening runs DFS with a depth limit of 0, then 1, then 2, … It finds the same shallow path as BFS while using only DFS's memory.

Definition: Repeat depth-bounded DFS (DB-DFS) with an increasing bound until the goal is found. DB-DFS does not expand nodes at depth equal to the bound.

Pseudocode:

```
for bound ← 0, 1, 2, …
    result ← DB-DFS(S, bound)      # DFS that does not expand nodes at depth = bound
    if result ≠ failure: return result
    if no node was cut off by the bound: return failure
```

- N(DFID) ≈ N(BFS) · b/(b−1): extra work is a small factor of BFS. Most nodes of a tree are on the last level, so repeating the upper levels is cheap.

Combines BFS's optimal depth with DFS's small memory; the repeated work is small for branching factors above 2.

Complete: yes. Optimal: yes for unit costs. Time: O(b^d). Space: O(b·d).

- Trap: Count expansions over all rounds, not just the last.
- Trap: Plain depth-bounded DFS with CLOSED can miss a goal inside the bound when a node was first reached by a deeper route; here DB-DFS reopens a node found again at a smaller depth, so the first bound that works is the true shallowest goal depth (try example graph-dfid-closed, and compare Depth-Bounded DFS there).
- Trap: DFID re-expands the upper levels in every round: on a wide graph that is a small overhead, on a thin chain it is large (try graph-dfs-deep and read the dry-run table).

## BFS on a state space (week 2, Graph search · uninformed)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/statespace-bfs.html

Water jugs, the 8-puzzle and missionaries-and-cannibals all have a start state, a goal test and a rule for the legal moves. Nobody draws their graph: MoveGen writes the neighbours of a state when asked. Breadth First Search explores in rings, so the first goal it picks is a solution with the fewest moves.

Definition: A state-space problem is (S, GoalTest, MoveGen). OPEN holds node pairs (state, parent, depth) that have been generated but not expanded; CLOSED holds those already expanded. BFS keeps OPEN as a queue. The goal test is applied when a node is picked from OPEN. A child that is already on OPEN or CLOSED is not added again, which is what makes this graph search rather than tree search. The parent in each pair lets us read the solution back.

Pseudocode:

```
OPEN ← [(S, nil, 0)];  CLOSED ← [ ]
while OPEN not empty
    (N, parent, d) ← head(OPEN);  remove it
    if GoalTest(N): return the path via parent pointers
    CLOSED ← (N, parent, d) : CLOSED
    children ← MoveGen(N) minus states on OPEN or CLOSED
    OPEN ← OPEN ++ [(C, N, d+1) for C in children]     # append = queue
return failure
```

- nodes ≤ 1 + b + b² + … + b^d: at most b^d states in the last ring. Every state in ring k has up to b children, so rings grow geometrically; CLOSED stops repeats from adding more.
- solution length = depth of the first goal picked: fewest moves. All states at depth k are picked before any at depth k + 1.

The water-jug problem (8, 5, 3 litres, aim for 4) has only 16 reachable states, so BFS finishes quickly and the answer, 7 pourings, is the shortest. On the 8-puzzle the rings grow fast, which is why informed search (A*) matters.

Complete: yes (finite state space). Optimal: yes, fewest moves (unit move cost). Time: O(b^d). Space: O(b^d).

- Trap: Without CLOSED the same state is generated again and again (pour A→B then B→A). Graph search cuts these cycles.
- Trap: The goal test is on picking from OPEN, not on generating, so the last ring is generated before the search stops.
- Trap: BFS needs memory for a whole ring: on example space-8-puzzle-12 (a 12-move board) it hits the 400-expansion cap long before the goal, while A* with Manhattan distance needs 16 expansions.
- Trap: Ties and the order of children follow MoveGen's order. A different order gives a different but equally short solution.

## DFS on a state space (week 2, Graph search · uninformed)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/statespace-dfs.html

Depth First Search follows one line of moves as far as it goes, and only when it hits a dead end (or a state it has seen) does it return to the most recent choice. On a state space with MoveGen in code this finds a solution fast, but not necessarily a short one.

Definition: The same node pairs (state, parent, depth) and the same OPEN/CLOSED lists as BFS, but OPEN is a stack: the children of the picked node are put at the front in MoveGen order, so the first child is picked next. The goal test is on picking. A child already on OPEN or CLOSED is not added again. An optional depth bound stops the dive.

Pseudocode:

```
OPEN ← [(S, nil, 0)];  CLOSED ← [ ]
while OPEN not empty
    (N, parent, d) ← head(OPEN);  remove it
    if GoalTest(N): return the path via parent pointers
    CLOSED ← (N, parent, d) : CLOSED
    if depth bound reached: continue
    children ← MoveGen(N) minus states on OPEN or CLOSED
    OPEN ← [(C, N, d+1) for C in children] ++ OPEN     # prepend = stack
return failure
```

- solution depth ≥ shortest depth d: a goal is found, maybe deep. DFS commits to the first child each time, so the first goal it reaches lies on whatever branch it dived into.

On the water-jug problem DFS reaches a state with 4 litres but often by a longer pouring sequence than BFS. On the 8-puzzle without a bound it can wander through thousands of states, which is why the studio has an expansion cap and an optional depth bound.

Complete: yes on a finite space with CLOSED. Optimal: no. Time: O(b^m). Space: linear on a tree; with CLOSED, all states seen.

- Trap: DFS is not optimal: on example space-jug-seven (7 litres in some jug) BFS needs 5 pourings, DFS 9. Run both and compare the solution tables.
- Trap: On the 8-puzzle DFS wanders: space-8-puzzle exhausts the 400-expansion cap without reaching a goal five moves away.
- Trap: Without CLOSED, DFS can loop forever on a state space with cycles (pour back and forth). CLOSED fixes that.
- Trap: With a depth bound and CLOSED, a state first reached by a deep path is closed and not retried by a shorter one, so the search can miss a solution within the bound (supplementary note).
- Trap: The order of children is MoveGen's order; a different order sends the dive down another branch.

## Simple search (no node pairs) (week 2, Graph search · uninformed)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/statespace-simple.html

The first search procedures in the course keep only states on OPEN. They answer 'is a goal reachable?' but not 'how do I get there?'. This tracer runs that version on a state space so you can see the answer arrive without a path.

Definition: OPEN is a list of states, CLOSED a list of states. Each loop picks the head of OPEN, tests it, moves it to CLOSED and adds its unseen children. Nothing records which state generated which, so when the goal is picked there is no chain of parents to follow. Replacing each state by a node pair (state, parent, depth) fixes that.

Pseudocode:

```
OPEN ← [S];  CLOSED ← [ ]
while OPEN not empty
    N ← head(OPEN);  remove it
    if GoalTest(N): return "goal reached"        # but by which moves?
    CLOSED ← N : CLOSED
    children ← MoveGen(N) minus states on OPEN or CLOSED
    OPEN ← OPEN ++ children  (queue)  or  children ++ OPEN  (stack)
return failure
```

- path recovery needs one pointer per state: parent(N). The path is the chain goal, parent(goal), parent(parent(goal)), … back to the start; with no pointers there is no chain.

This is the motivation for node pairs: one extra field per entry turns 'a goal exists' into 'here is a solution'.

Complete: yes (finite space, with CLOSED). Optimal: n/a: no path is returned. Time: as BFS / DFS. Space: as BFS / DFS.

- Trap: Reaching the goal is not the same as having the solution. For puzzles the moves are the answer: run this on space-water-jug and the last step says the path is lost, while BFS on the same problem prints the 7 pourings.
- Trap: Switching OPEN between queue and stack changes how many states are expanded (15 for the queue, 9 for the stack on space-water-jug) but never recovers the path.
- Trap: Without CLOSED (not offered here) the procedure may never stop on a cyclic state space.

## Hill climbing in the blocks world (h1 vs h2) (week 3, Planning)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/plan-hill-climbing.html

Here a state is a set of stacks and a move takes the top block of one stack and puts it on the table or on top of another stack. The heuristic is only as good as the information it holds: h1 looks at each block's immediate support, h2 looks at the entire structure beneath it. Same search, same moves, different heuristic: one gets stuck, the other solves the problem.

Definition: Steepest-ascent hill climbing: move to the best neighbour as long as it is strictly better than the current state. h1 gives +1 to a block that sits on the right thing (the table for a bottom block) and −1 otherwise. h2 gives a block +k when it and the k−1 blocks below it all stand on the right things, and −k (its height in the stack) otherwise. The goal scores n under h1 and n(n+1)/2 for a single tower under h2. (The exact course picture is not reproduced here; this is the standard construction of the example.)

Pseudocode:

```
N ← start
loop
    pick the neighbour M (move one top block to the table or onto another stack) with the highest h(M)
    if h(M) ≤ h(N): return N      // local maximum or plateau: stuck
    N ← M
    if N is the goal: return N

h1(N) = Σ over blocks: +1 if on the thing it should be on in the goal, −1 otherwise
h2(N) = Σ over blocks: +k if its whole structure of k blocks (down to the table) is right, −k otherwise
```

- h1 = Σ ±1 per block, + if on the right thing: count blocks that are locally right. Cheap, but a block resting on a wrongly built tower still scores +1, so dismantling that tower looks like a loss.
- h2 = Σ ±k per block, + if its whole support structure is correct: credit a correct structure of k blocks with k, penalise a wrong one with k. A wrongly placed block pulls down everything above it, so dismantling a wrong tower is rewarded and building a right one is rewarded more with height.

The same algorithm with a different evaluation function turns failure into success: the quality of the heuristic decides whether a hill-climber can find the goal.

Complete: no. Optimal: no. Time: one pass over the neighbours per move. Space: O(1) states.

- Trap: A block that is on the right thing is not necessarily correct: if what it stands on is wrong, h2 counts it as wrong.
- Trap: Stuck does not mean the goal is unreachable: it means no single move improves h.
- Trap: The goal is read from on(x,y) and ontable(x) facts; a block with no fact is assumed to belong on the table.

## Brute force (exact) (week 3, TSP · exact)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-brute-force.html

The travelling salesperson problem (TSP) asks for the shortest round trip that visits every city exactly once. Brute force simply tries every possible round trip and keeps the shortest. It is the only method here that is guaranteed to find the best tour, and it is how every other method's answer is checked.

Definition: Fix the first city (a round trip can start anywhere), list every ordering of the remaining n−1 cities, compute each tour's cost, and return the cheapest.

Pseudocode:

```
best ← ∞
for every permutation p of cities 2..n   (symmetric: skip p with p[first] > p[last])
    if cost(city1 + p) < best: best ← that tour
return best
```

- number of tours = (n−1)! / 2  (symmetric): fix one city, order the rest, halve for direction. Rotations of a cycle are the same tour, and so is the reversed cycle when C(i,j) = C(j,i).
- cost(T) = Σ C(tᵢ, tᵢ₊₁) + C(tₙ, t₁): add up every edge on the cycle. The closing edge back to the start is part of the tour; forgetting it is the most common arithmetic slip.

It works because it leaves nothing out. It fails in practice because (n−1)!/2 explodes: 60 tours for 6 cities, 181,440 for 10, about 10^155 for 100.

Complete: yes. Optimal: yes. Time: O(n!). Space: O(n).

- Trap: Forgetting the closing edge.
- Trap: Counting (n−1)! instead of (n−1)!/2 for a symmetric instance.
- Trap: Using brute force on large n: the studio limits it to 9 cities.

## Brute force (truth table) (week 3, SAT · exact)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/sat-brute-force.html

A SAT instance asks for an assignment of true or false to every variable that makes every clause true. With n variables there are 2ⁿ assignments, so the most direct method is to try them all. This is the baseline against which the local-search methods of this week are measured.

Definition: Treat the assignment as a bit string (bit i = 1 means variable i is true). Enumerate every bit string, evaluate every clause, and record h = the number of satisfied clauses. A string with h = m satisfies the formula.

Pseudocode:

```
for each bit string X of length n, in counting order 00…0, 00…1, …
    h(X) ← number of clauses satisfied by X
    if h(X) = m: X is a solution
return the solutions (or, if none, the rows with the largest h)
```

- |search space| = 2ⁿ: two choices per variable. This is why n is limited to 6 here: 2⁶ = 64 rows still fit on a screen; 2²⁰ is already a million.
- h(X) = Σᵢ [clauseᵢ satisfied by X]: the heuristic is the number of true clauses. The same h guides every local-search method in this section; local search tries to climb to h = m without enumerating the table.

Brute force is complete and exact, which makes it the reference answer: every local-search result can be checked against its truth table. Its cost is the reason local search exists.

Complete: yes. Optimal: yes (finds every solution). Time: O(2ⁿ · m). Space: O(n).

- Trap: A solution is h = m (all clauses), not just a high h.
- Trap: There can be several solutions, or none; do not stop at the first unless asked.
- Trap: The truth table grows as 2ⁿ: adding one variable doubles it.
- Trap: No row with h = m proves the formula unsatisfiable: on sat-unsat the best rows have h = 4 of 5 clauses, and brute force can say 'none' for certain. Local search failing says nothing of the kind.

## Nearest Neighbour (week 3, TSP · constructive)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-nearest-neighbour.html

Nearest Neighbour is what most people do by hand: from where you are, go to the closest place you have not visited yet. It builds a tour quickly but can paint itself into a corner and pay for a long trip home at the end.

Definition: A constructive (synthesis) heuristic: start at a given city, repeatedly append the nearest unvisited city, and finally return to the start.

Pseudocode:

```
tour ← [start]
while unvisited cities remain
    c ← last city of tour
    append the unvisited city nearest to c   (ties: alphabetical)
return tour   (closing edge back to start is implied)
```

- next = argmin over unvisited j of C(c, j): pick the cheapest edge out of the current city that leads somewhere new. Each choice is locally best; nothing guarantees the sum of choices is globally best.
- NN ≤ ½(⌈log₂ n⌉ + 1) · OPT  (metric TSP): in the worst case NN can be about log n times worse than optimal. Bad cases exist where greedy local moves strand far-away cities.

Cheap and intuitive. Its weakness is the end game: the last cities are whatever is left over, often far apart, and the forced return edge can be the longest edge in the tour. It always returns a tour, but never promises an optimal one.

Complete: always returns a tour. Optimal: no. Time: O(n²). Space: O(n).

- Trap: The tour depends on the start city: run it from every city and keep the best. On Six cities (examples) the tour costs 264 from A (its forced return leg B→A = 92 is the longest edge) but 240 from C, and the optimum is 224 (try the start city setting).
- Trap: Do not forget the forced return edge in the cost.
- Trap: Write the answer in path representation starting from the asked city.

## Hill climbing (N1) (week 3, SAT · local search)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/sat-hill-climbing.html

Local search treats the assignments as states and a flip of one variable as a move. The heuristic h counts satisfied clauses, so a solution is a state with h = m. Hill climbing walks uphill on h and never accepts a step that does not strictly improve it.

Definition: The neighbourhood N1 of a bit string is the n strings that differ from it in exactly one bit. Pick the neighbour with the highest h (ties go to the lowest bit, i.e. the alphabetically first variable). Move only if its h is strictly greater than the current h; otherwise stop.

Pseudocode:

```
N ← start
loop
    if h(N) = m: return N                      # solved
    nbrs ← all strings obtained by flipping one bit of N     # N1
    B ← the neighbour with the largest h (ties: lowest bit)
    if h(B) > h(N): N ← B
    else: return N                             # local maximum or plateau
```

- |N1| = C(n,1) = n: n neighbours per state. Each iteration costs n evaluations of h.
- move iff h(B) > h(N): strictly better only. This rule is what makes the method stop on plateaus; tabu search and simulated annealing relax it.

It is cheap and often gets close, but a state whose neighbours are all no better is a trap even when h < m. On the course example it climbs 0000 (h 4) → 1000 (h 5) and stops, although 1101 (h 6) is a solution two flips away.

Complete: no. Optimal: no. Time: O(n · m) per move. Space: O(n).

- Trap: Stopping with h < m does not mean the formula is unsatisfiable, only that this start is stuck.
- Trap: Equal h is not an improvement: a plateau stops strict hill climbing.
- Trap: Ties between equally good neighbours go to the lowest bit; a different rule can give a different path.
- Trap: Two different traps: on a plateau some neighbour has equal h, at a strict local maximum every neighbour is worse. The captions say which one. Course example sat-four-var stops on a plateau (1000: three neighbours with h 5); the example 'Local-maximum trap' (sat-local-trap) stops at 0100, where all four neighbours have h 6.

## Greedy heuristic (week 3, TSP · constructive)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-greedy.html

The Greedy heuristic builds the tour out of the shortest edges available anywhere on the map, like snapping together the closest pairs of cities first. Two rules keep the pieces from becoming something other than one big loop.

Definition: Sort all edges by length. Accept an edge unless it would give a city a third edge (degree 3) or close a loop before all cities are included (premature cycle). Stop at n edges.

Pseudocode:

```
sort all edges by length (ties: alphabetical)
for each edge (a,b)
    if degree(a) = 2 or degree(b) = 2: reject
    if a, b already connected and fewer than n−1 edges chosen: reject (premature cycle)
    else accept
read the tour from the chosen edges, starting at the given city
```

- accept (a,b) ⇔ deg(a) < 2 ∧ deg(b) < 2 ∧ (find(a) ≠ find(b) ∨ |E| = n−1): both ends have a free slot, and they are in different fragments unless this is the closing edge. These are exactly the conditions for the chosen edges to still be part of some Hamiltonian cycle.
- cost = Σ of accepted edge lengths: the tour cost is just the accepted edges. Greedy accepts exactly n edges.

Short edges are likely to belong to good tours, so Greedy usually beats Nearest Neighbour. But fragments are joined late, and the final edges are whatever remains legal, which can be very long.

Complete: always returns a tour. Optimal: no. Time: O(n² log n). Space: O(n²).

- Trap: Track degrees and fragments carefully; most exam errors are an illegal acceptance.
- Trap: The last accepted edge is forced and may be long.
- Trap: 'Greedy from city X' only changes where you start writing the tour.
- Trap: Watch both rejection reasons on Six cities (examples): CE = 31 is refused as a premature cycle (A–C–E would close a triangle), CF, BD, AD … are refused because a city would get a degree of 3. The result, 238, is not the optimum 224.

## Beam search (week 3, SAT · local search)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/sat-beam.html

Hill climbing follows a single path and so can be trapped. Beam search keeps a small population of w assignments: the w best of everything reachable in one flip from the current beam. A wider beam explores more routes at the cost of w times more work per level.

Definition: Level 0 is [start]. At each level, generate the N1 neighbours of every assignment in the beam (removing duplicates), sort them by h, and keep the best w. Stop when no solution appears and the best h of the new beam is not higher than that of the old one; return the best assignment seen.

Pseudocode:

```
OPEN ← [start]                       # the beam, best first
loop
    if some X in OPEN has h(X) = m: return X
    cand ← distinct N1 neighbours of every X in OPEN
    OPEN ← the w best of cand by h (ties: order of generation, lowest bit first)
    if h(head of OPEN) ≤ h(previous head): stop
return the best assignment seen
```

- |cand| ≤ w · n: at most w·n candidates per level. The work per level is linear in the beam width.
- w = 1 ⇒ hill climbing; w ≥ 2ⁿ ⇒ breadth-first over the whole space: the width interpolates between the two. The same dial as in graph and TSP beam search.

The beam lets a runner-up survive. Hill climbing keeps only the single best neighbour, but the second-best string may have a neighbour that beats everything reachable from the best one. On the example 'Local-maximum trap' (sat-local-trap) from 0000: w = 1 is hill climbing and stops at 0100 (h 7); w = 2 also keeps 0001 (h 7), and its neighbour 0011 has h 8, a solution, at level 2. The beam is still incomplete: it stops as soon as the head does not improve, so it cannot cross a plateau, and if all w members fall into the same basin it stalls like hill climbing. On the course example sat-four-var even w = 4 stops at 1000 (h 5), because the head of the beam does not improve at level 2.

Complete: no. Optimal: no. Time: O(levels · w · n · m). Space: O(w · n).

- Trap: The beam holds the w best of all neighbours together, not w neighbours per member.
- Trap: Remove duplicate neighbours, or the beam fills up with copies of the same string.
- Trap: Stopping rule: the head not improving. A level whose beam is merely as good as the last one ends the search, so a wider beam does not help on a plateau (try sat-four-var with w = 1 to 4).
- Trap: A wider beam is not always better; it costs w times more evaluations and only helps when a runner-up leads somewhere the best member does not.

## Savings heuristic (week 3, TSP · constructive)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-savings.html

Imagine a delivery van that returns to the depot after every single delivery. The Savings heuristic starts there and asks: which two trips can I combine to save the most driving? It keeps combining trips until there is just one round trip.

Definition: Choose a base (fulcrum) city b. For each pair of other cities compute the saving S(i,j) of visiting i and j on one trip instead of two. Process pairs from the largest saving down, linking i and j whenever both are still ends of different sub-tours.

Pseudocode:

```
for every pair i, j ≠ base:  S(i,j) ← C(base,i) + C(base,j) − C(i,j)
sort pairs by S, largest first (ties: alphabetical)
start with n−1 sub-tours base–x–base
for each pair (i,j) in that order
    if i and j are ends of different sub-tours: link i–j (merge)
    else: skip (same sub-tour, or an interior city)
return the single tour
```

- S(i,j) = C(b,i) + C(b,j) − C(i,j): trip b→i→b plus b→j→b, minus going i→j directly. Merging two out-and-back trips replaces the two edges i–b and b–j with one edge i–j; the difference is the distance saved.
- cost = 2·Σₓ C(b,x) − Σ accepted S(i,j): start with all out-and-back trips, subtract each saving you used. Every merge removes exactly its saving from the total, which is a quick way to check your final tour cost.

Savings rewards pairs that are far from the base but close to each other, which avoids stranding remote cities. It is usually the best of the three constructive heuristics, but the result depends on the base city and on tie-breaking.

Complete: always returns a tour. Optimal: no. Time: O(n² log n). Space: O(n²).

- Trap: The savings formula has a minus on C(i,j), not on the base distances.
- Trap: A pair is refused if either city is interior, even if they are in different sub-tours.
- Trap: Know which pairs merged and which did not: exams ask for the first three of each (Six cities, base A: merged BF, BD, CF; refused DF, BC, CD).
- Trap: The result depends on the base city: on Six cities base A gives 224 (the optimum) but base E gives 229, and there AD (S = 42) is refused because D is already interior, not because of a cycle.

## Variable Neighbourhood Descent (N1 → N1–n) (week 3, SAT · local search)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/sat-vnd.html

A local maximum depends on the neighbourhood: a state can have no better one-flip neighbour and still have a better string two flips away. VND uses that. It searches the small, cheap neighbourhood first and only widens it when it is stuck.

Definition: Let Nk be the strings that differ from the current one in exactly k bits, so |Nk| = C(n,k), and let N1–k = N1 ∪ … ∪ Nk. Start with k = 1. Move to the best member of N1–k if it is strictly better, and reset k to 1. Otherwise increase k. When k passes n, the state is a local maximum of every neighbourhood, hence a global maximum of h (N1–n is the whole space).

Pseudocode:

```
N ← start;  k ← 1
while k ≤ n and h(N) < m
    nbrs ← all strings that differ from N in at most k bits     # N1–k
    B ← the neighbour with the largest h (ties: fewest flips, then lowest bit)
    if h(B) > h(N): N ← B;  k ← 1
    else: k ← k + 1
return N
```

- |Nk| = C(n,k): choose which k of the n bits to flip. This is why the neighbourhoods grow so fast: for n = 4 the sizes are 4, 6, 4, 1.
- |N1–k| = C(n,1) + … + C(n,k): cumulative size. |N1–n| = 2ⁿ − 1, so the last phase is brute force: VND ends exactly at a global maximum, at brute-force cost in the worst case.

On the course example, hill climbing stops at 1000 (h 5), but flipping the pair b, d reaches 1101 (h 6), a solution. VND finds it by widening to N1–2 at 1000. Most of the time the cheap neighbourhood does the work and the expensive ones are only paid for when needed. The same escape works at a strict local maximum: on 'Local-maximum trap' (sat-local-trap) N1 fails at 0100 (all four neighbours have h 6) and N1–2 flips c and d to reach the solution 0111. The first step lists the sizes C(n,k): 4, 6, 4, 1 for four variables, 6, 15, 20, 15, 6, 1 for the six-variable sat-random-3sat; set the largest neighbourhood to 1 to see plain hill climbing fail.

Complete: yes if run up to N1–n (it then covers the space). Optimal: yes with N1–n. Time: up to O(2ⁿ · m). Space: O(n).

- Trap: After an improvement return to N1, not to the neighbourhood that found it.
- Trap: N1–2 contains the one-flip neighbours as well as the pairs: 4 + 6 = 10 strings for n = 4, not 6.
- Trap: If the whole sequence fails the result is a true global maximum of h, but a global maximum with h < m means the formula is unsatisfiable.

## 2-city exchange (week 3, TSP · perturbation)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-two-city-exchange.html

Perturbative methods start from a complete tour and improve it by small changes. 2-city exchange is one such change: swap the positions of two cities. Repeating the best improving change until none helps is hill climbing, and where it stops is a local optimum.

Definition: MoveGen(2-city exchange) lists every tour reachable by one 2-city exchange move (n(n−1)/2 neighbours). Steepest-descent hill climbing moves to the best neighbour while it is strictly better than the current tour.

Pseudocode:

```
node ← start tour
loop
    neighbours ← MoveGen(node)          # swap two cities (4 edges change; 2 if adjacent)
    best ← cheapest neighbour
    if cost(best) ≥ cost(node): return node   (local optimum)
    node ← best
```

- |N₂c| = n(n−1)/2: choose any two positions to swap. Swapping cities i and j changes up to 4 edges; if they are adjacent only 2 change.

Hill climbing is fast and always improves until it stops, but it stops at the first tour with no better neighbour. A denser neighbourhood has fewer such traps but costs more per step.

Complete: no. Optimal: no (local optimum). Time: n(n−1)/2 evaluations per step. Space: O(n).

- Trap: Hill climbing stops when no neighbour is strictly better, even if equal-cost neighbours exist (a plateau).
- Trap: A local optimum is not the global one: on Six cities, started from the Greedy tour (238), 2-city exchange stops at 229, the optimum is 224. Variable neighbourhood descent continues from such a tour with a different move.
- Trap: Count neighbours with the right formula for the operator.
- Trap: In an asymmetric TSP a 2-edge move reverses a block, so many edge costs change.

## Best First Search (week 3, Graph search · informed)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-best-first.html

Best First Search uses a heuristic h(N), a guess of the distance from N to the goal, and always expands the node that looks closest to the goal.

Definition: A state-space search problem has a start node S, a goal test, and a MoveGen function that lists the neighbours of a node. The search keeps two lists: OPEN (nodes generated but not yet expanded) and CLOSED (nodes already expanded). Each entry is a node pair (node, parent, value) so the path can be read back through parents. OPEN is ordered by h(N).

Pseudocode:

```
OPEN ← [(S, nil, h(S))] ordered by h
while OPEN not empty
    N ← node with least h;  remove it
    if GoalTest(N): return the path
    move N to CLOSED
    add children not on OPEN or CLOSED, ordered by h
```

- pick argmin h on OPEN: most promising-looking node first. Fast when h is accurate, but it ignores g, so the path found can be expensive.

Often reaches the goal quickly, but is not optimal and can be misled by a poor heuristic.

Complete: finite graphs. Optimal: no. Time: O(b^m) worst case. Space: O(b^m).

- Trap: Best First ignores g, so it is not optimal even when h is admissible: on graph-greedy-detour it takes S–A–G (cost 11) and never looks at the cost-4 route S–B–G; on graph-weighted it returns cost 13 where UCS finds 12. A* adds g.
- Trap: Ties in h decide the path: state your tie-breaking.

## Best neighbour, fixed moves (week 3, SAT · local search)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/sat-best-neighbour.html

Hill climbing quits when no neighbour is better. A simple escape is to keep moving anyway: take the best neighbour even if it is worse or equal, for a fixed number of moves, and remember the best string seen. The trouble is that the best neighbour of a state is often the state we just left.

Definition: At each of the k moves, evaluate the N1 neighbours of the current string, move to the one with the highest h (ties to the lowest bit) regardless of whether h improves, and update the best string seen. Return the best string seen.

Pseudocode:

```
N ← start;  bestSeen ← N
repeat for a fixed number of moves
    B ← the N1 neighbour with the largest h (ties: lowest bit)
    N ← B                                   # even if h(B) ≤ h(N)
    if h(N) > h(bestSeen): bestSeen ← N
return bestSeen
```

- N′ = argmax over N1(N) of h: the best neighbour, uphill or not. Flipping a variable back and forth keeps being the best choice, so the walk can cycle: x → y → x → y …

It shows why memory is needed. From the solution 1101 on the course example the best neighbour is 0101 (h 5) and from there the best neighbour is 1101 again: a cycle of length 2. Tabu search forbids the move back for a few iterations to break such cycles. The cycle also appears while still unsolved: on 'Local-maximum trap' (sat-local-trap) the walk goes 0000 → 0100 (h 7) → 1100 (h 6, downhill) → 0100 → 1100 … and never reaches the solutions 0011 or 0111, because 0100 is always the best neighbour of 1100.

Complete: no. Optimal: no. Time: moves × n × m. Space: O(n).

- Trap: The last string is not the answer; the best string seen is.
- Trap: A revisited string means a cycle: from then on the walk repeats forever.
- Trap: With a solution reached the walk would normally stop; turn the stop off to watch the cycling.

## 2-edge exchange (2-opt) (week 3, TSP · perturbation)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-two-edge-exchange.html

Perturbative methods start from a complete tour and improve it by small changes. 2-edge exchange is one such change: remove two non-adjacent edges and reconnect. Repeating the best improving change until none helps is hill climbing, and where it stops is a local optimum.

Definition: MoveGen(2-edge exchange) lists every tour reachable by one 2-edge exchange move (n(n−3)/2 neighbours). Steepest-descent hill climbing moves to the best neighbour while it is strictly better than the current tour.

Pseudocode:

```
node ← start tour
loop
    neighbours ← MoveGen(node)          # remove (a,b),(c,d); add (a,c),(b,d); reverse the block
    best ← cheapest neighbour
    if cost(best) ≥ cost(node): return node   (local optimum)
    node ← best
```

- |N₂e| = n(n−3)/2: pairs of edges that do not share a city. Each of n edges can pair with n−3 non-adjacent edges; each pair is counted twice.
- Δ = C(a,c) + C(b,d) − C(a,b) − C(c,d): new edges minus removed edges. Only four edges change, so a move is evaluated in O(1) without recomputing the whole tour.

Hill climbing is fast and always improves until it stops, but it stops at the first tour with no better neighbour. A denser neighbourhood has fewer such traps but costs more per step.

Complete: no. Optimal: no (local optimum). Time: n(n−3)/2 evaluations per step. Space: O(n).

- Trap: Hill climbing stops when no neighbour is strictly better, even if equal-cost neighbours exist (a plateau).
- Trap: A local optimum is not the global one: on Six cities, started from the Greedy tour (238), 2-opt stops at 229 although the optimum is 224 (the last step says so). Started from the Nearest-neighbour tour it reaches 224, so the start matters.
- Trap: Count neighbours with the right formula for the operator.
- Trap: In an asymmetric TSP a 2-edge move reverses a block, so many edge costs change.

## Hill Climbing (week 3, Graph search · informed)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-hill-climbing.html

Hill climbing is the simplest way to use a heuristic: always step to the neighbour that looks closest to the goal, and stop when no neighbour looks better than where you are. It needs almost no memory, but it can stop on a hilltop that is not the summit.

Definition: From the current node move to the child with the smallest h, provided it is strictly smaller than h(current). Otherwise stop and return the current node.

Pseudocode:

```
node ← start
newNode ← head(sort_h(MoveGen(node)))
while h(newNode) < h(node)
    node ← newNode
    newNode ← head(sort_h(MoveGen(node)))
return node
```

- next = argmin over children C of h(C), accepted only if h(next) < h(current): go to the best-looking child only if it is better than here. Greedy local improvement; there is no memory to back up from a dead end.

Constant memory and very fast, but incomplete: local optima, plateaus and ridges stop it. The fixes are exactly the Week 3 ideas: beam search, random restarts, tabu memory, simulated annealing.

Complete: no. Optimal: no. Time: O(b) per step. Space: O(1).

- Trap: Hill climbing never backtracks: on example graph-hill-trap it climbs to L (h = 1), a dead end, and stops with the goal unreached although S–B–C–G exists.
- Trap: A plateau (equal h) stops the course version: try example graph-plateau, where B has the same h as A.
- Trap: Reaching a node with h = 0 that is not the goal means h is misleading there.
- Trap: Even when it reaches the goal, the path need not be cheapest: on graph-greedy-detour it takes the cheap-looking edge with cost 10 (it uses only h, never the cost g).

## Or-opt (move a city) (week 3, TSP · perturbation)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-or-opt.html

Perturbative methods start from a complete tour and improve it by small changes. Or-opt is one such change: move one city to another place in the tour. Repeating the best improving change until none helps is hill climbing, and where it stops is a local optimum.

Definition: MoveGen(Or-opt) lists every tour reachable by one Or-opt move (about n² neighbours). Steepest-descent hill climbing moves to the best neighbour while it is strictly better than the current tour.

Pseudocode:

```
node ← start tour
loop
    neighbours ← MoveGen(node)          # remove a city, reinsert it elsewhere
    best ← cheapest neighbour
    if cost(best) ≥ cost(node): return node   (local optimum)
    node ← best
```

- Δ = C(p,q) − C(p,c) − C(c,q) + C(x,c) + C(c,y) − C(x,y): take c out from between p and q, put it between x and y. Moving one city removes three edges and adds three, so Or-opt moves are a subset of 3-edge exchanges.

Hill climbing is fast and always improves until it stops, but it stops at the first tour with no better neighbour. A denser neighbourhood has fewer such traps but costs more per step.

Complete: no. Optimal: no (local optimum). Time: about n² evaluations per step. Space: O(n).

- Trap: Hill climbing stops when no neighbour is strictly better, even if equal-cost neighbours exist (a plateau).
- Trap: A different move set has different local optima: on Six cities from the Greedy tour (238) Or-opt reaches the optimum 224, where 2-opt and 2-city exchange both stop at 229.
- Trap: Count neighbours with the right formula for the operator.
- Trap: In an asymmetric TSP a 2-edge move reverses a block, so many edge costs change.

## Beam Search (week 3, Graph search · informed)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-beam.html

Beam search is breadth-first search on a diet: at every level it keeps only the w most promising nodes by h and forgets the rest. A wider beam is safer, a narrower one is cheaper.

Definition: Level by level, generate the children of every node in the beam, discard those seen before, and keep the w with the smallest h. Succeed when the goal enters the beam; fail when no new children remain.

Pseudocode:

```
OPEN ← [start]
while goal not in OPEN
    children ← MoveGen of every node in OPEN, minus nodes seen before
    if children is empty: return failure
    OPEN ← the w best of children by h
return the goal's path
```

- memory ≤ w per level: the beam width bounds the frontier. That is the whole point: predictable memory. w = 1 is hill climbing except that it keeps moving even when the best child is worse (and fails only when no unseen child is left); w = ∞ is breadth-first search.

Keeps several alternatives alive, so one bad estimate does not end the search, but anything outside the beam is lost forever.

Complete: no. Optimal: no. Time: O(w · b · d). Space: O(w · d).

- Trap: Beam search is incomplete: the only path to the goal can fall outside the beam. On graph-hill-trap, w = 1 keeps only L and runs out of new nodes (fails); w = 2 keeps B too and reaches G. Change w and compare.
- Trap: Ties in h decide which nodes survive.
- Trap: A wider beam is not always cheaper or shorter: w only changes which nodes survive, it never optimises cost.

## Tabu search (week 3, SAT · local search)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/sat-tabu.html

Best-neighbour walking cycles because the best move is often the one that undoes the last. Tabu search adds a short-term memory: a variable that has just been flipped may not be flipped again for a few iterations, which forces the walk onward, even through worse or equal states.

Definition: At every iteration choose the best flip that is not tabu and take it even if h gets worse. The flipped variable becomes tabu for the tenure tt iterations. A tabu flip is still allowed when it gives an h larger than the best seen (the aspiration criterion). Optionally a long-term frequency memory subtracts λ times the number of past flips of a variable from its score, steering the search towards variables rarely flipped.

Pseudocode:

```
N ← start;  bestSeen ← N
for t = 1, 2, …
    if h(N) = m: stop
    rank the one-bit flips i by  score(i) = h(flip(N,i)) − λ · freq(i)    (ties: lowest bit)
    take the first flip that is not tabu,
         or is tabu but gives h > h(bestSeen)             # aspiration
    N ← flip(N,i);  tabu(i) ← t + tt;  freq(i) ← freq(i) + 1
    if h(N) > h(bestSeen): bestSeen ← N
return bestSeen
```

- tabu(i) at iteration t ⇔ t ≤ tabuUntil(i),  tabuUntil(i) = t₀ + tt: flipped at t₀, forbidden for the next tt iterations. Too short a tenure lets the walk cycle; too long blocks good moves. On the course example tt = 2 is enough to get out.
- allow a tabu flip if h(new) > h(bestSeen): aspiration criterion. Tabu exists to stop cycling, never to block a new record.
- score(i) = h(flip(N,i)) − λ · freq(i): frequency penalty (**supplementary**: the weight λ is a common implementation choice, not fixed by the course). Long-term memory of how often each variable has been flipped diversifies the search; λ = 0 switches it off.

From 0000 on the course example: flip a (→ 1000, h 5); a is now tabu, and the best remaining flips tie at h 5, so b (the lowest bit) gives 1100, a sideways move; from 1100, a and b are tabu, and flipping d gives 1101, h 6, the unique solution. Hill climbing could never take the sideways move, and best-neighbour walking would have gone back to 0000. The tenure matters. On 'Local-maximum trap' (sat-local-trap) tenure 1 only forbids the immediate undo and the walk goes round 0000 → 0100 → 1100 → 1000 → 0000 and never finds a solution; tenure 2 breaks the loop and reaches 0111 in 5 flips. With tenure 4 and aspiration off every flip becomes tabu at 1111 and the search stops; with aspiration on, the tabu flip of a is allowed because 0111 (h 8) beats the best h seen (7).

Complete: no. Optimal: no. Time: iterations × n × m. Space: O(n).

- Trap: The tabu element is the variable (the move), not the whole string.
- Trap: Tabu takes the best allowed move even when h decreases; only bestSeen is monotone.
- Trap: Apply aspiration before rejecting a tabu flip.
- Trap: With tenure 2 a variable flipped at iteration 1 is still tabu at iterations 2 and 3 and free again at 4.
- Trap: Too short a tenure cycles (tenure 1 on sat-local-trap), too long a tenure freezes the search (tenure 4 with aspiration off stops when every flip is tabu). Aspiration is what rescues a record-breaking move from a long tenure.

## 3-edge exchange (week 3, TSP · perturbation)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-three-edge-exchange.html

Perturbative methods start from a complete tour and improve it by small changes. 3-edge exchange is one such change: remove three edges and reconnect the segments. Repeating the best improving change until none helps is hill climbing, and where it stops is a local optimum.

Definition: MoveGen(3-edge exchange) lists every tour reachable by one 3-edge exchange move (O(n³) neighbours). Steepest-descent hill climbing moves to the best neighbour while it is strictly better than the current tour.

Pseudocode:

```
node ← start tour
loop
    neighbours ← MoveGen(node)          # remove three edges, reconnect segments
    best ← cheapest neighbour
    if cost(best) ≥ cost(node): return node   (local optimum)
    node ← best
```

- |N₃e| = O(n³): choose three edges, then a reconnection. Many more neighbours than 2-edge exchange, so more work per step; the extra moves reach tours that a 2-edge descent cannot.

Hill climbing is fast and always improves until it stops, but it stops at the first tour with no better neighbour. A 3-edge move changes all three edges it touches (the studio lists only these pure moves, not the 2-opt ones), so its local optima differ from 2-opt's: it is most useful after a 2-edge descent, which is what variable neighbourhood descent does.

Complete: no. Optimal: no (local optimum). Time: O(n³) evaluations per step. Space: O(n).

- Trap: Hill climbing stops when no neighbour is strictly better, even if equal-cost neighbours exist (a plateau).
- Trap: Do not assume a 3-edge local optimum is also a 2-edge local optimum: on Six cities from the Nearest-neighbour tour pure 3-edge exchange stops at 229 while 2-edge exchange from the same tour reaches 224. From the 2-opt optimum 229 (Greedy start) a 3-edge move does reach 224: see variable neighbourhood descent.
- Trap: Count neighbours with the right formula for the operator.
- Trap: In an asymmetric TSP a 2-edge move reverses a block, so many edge costs change.

## Variable neighbourhood descent (week 3, TSP · local search)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-vnd.html

If hill climbing gets stuck, one fix is to look further: use a bigger neighbourhood. Variable Neighbourhood Descent does this in order, from cheap and sparse to expensive and dense, so most of the improvement comes cheaply.

Definition: Given MoveGen functions ordered by density, hill climb with MoveGen(1) to a local optimum, then continue from there with MoveGen(2), and so on.

Pseudocode:

```
node ← start
for i ← 1 to n
    moveGen ← MoveGen(i)            # sparse → dense
    node ← HillClimbing(node, moveGen)
return node
```

- local optimum of N₁  ⇏  local optimum of N₂: being stuck in one neighbourhood does not mean being stuck in another. Different moves reach different tours; a denser neighbourhood contains moves the sparse one lacks.

Sparse neighbourhoods are cheap and do most of the work; dense ones are used only near the end, where they escape the sparse operator's traps.

Complete: no. Optimal: no. Time: sum of the phases' hill climbs. Space: O(n).

- Trap: The course version runs each MoveGen once, in order; some variants restart from MoveGen(1) after any improvement.
- Trap: A phase can make no progress at all: that is fine.
- Trap: Six cities from the Greedy tour (default order): 2-edge 238→229, 2-city 229→229 (no progress), 3-edge 229→224, the optimum. 2-opt alone is stuck at 229.

## Random walk (week 3, SAT · stochastic)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/sat-random-walk.html

Hill climbing is trapped by local maxima; the opposite extreme is a walk that ignores h entirely. A random walk picks a neighbour uniformly at random and always moves there. It explores everything eventually, but only by luck does it hit a solution.

Definition: From the current string choose one of the n one-flip neighbours uniformly at random (using the seeded generator) and move to it. Keep a record of the best string met on the way.

Pseudocode:

```
N ← start;  bestSeen ← N
repeat k times
    i ← random bit index
    N ← N with bit i flipped            # always accepted
    if h(N) > h(bestSeen): bestSeen ← N
return bestSeen
```

- P(pick bit i) = 1/n: every neighbour equally likely. That is what 'uniformly at random' means; h plays no part in the choice.

It is the baseline against which the other stochastic methods are judged: stochastic hill climbing and simulated annealing keep the randomness but let h bias the acceptance. On the ten-variable example sat-ten-var, 30 steps from 0000000000 find a solution for only 7 of 100 seeds, against 51 of 100 for simulated annealing (seed 2: the walk ends at h 46 of 48, annealing solves it).

Complete: no. Optimal: no. Time: k steps. Space: O(n).

- Trap: Different seeds give different walks; compare methods over several seeds.
- Trap: It may step straight off a solution; return bestSeen, not the last string.
- Trap: It can revisit the same strings: the walk has no memory (tabu search adds one).

## Beam search (week 3, TSP · local search)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-beam.html

Hill climbing follows one path. Beam search keeps a few of the best candidates at each level, a beam of width w, so a slightly worse option that leads somewhere better is not thrown away immediately.

Definition: OPEN holds w tours. Each level, generate the neighbours of all tours in OPEN, keep the w best as the new OPEN, and stop when the best of the level is no better than the best seen before.

Pseudocode:

```
OPEN ← [start];  N ← start
do
    bestEver ← N
    neighbours ← MoveGen(OPEN)        # of every node in OPEN, duplicates merged
    OPEN ← the w best of neighbours
    N ← head(OPEN)
while cost(N) < cost(bestEver)
return bestEver
```

- memory = w, work per level ≈ w · |N|: width times neighbourhood size. Beam search trades memory for robustness; w = 1 is hill climbing, w = ∞ approaches breadth-first search.

Keeping alternatives lets the search survive one bad step. A narrow beam can still miss the path to the optimum; a wide one costs more.

Complete: no. Optimal: no. Time: w · |N| per level. Space: O(w).

- Trap: w = 1 behaves exactly like hill climbing.
- Trap: Merge duplicate tours when generating neighbours of several beam members.
- Trap: Stopping is on the level's best, not on any member improving.
- Trap: The width matters: Six cities from the Greedy tour with 2-city exchange gives 229 for w = 1 (plain hill climbing) and w = 2, but 224 (the optimum) for w = 3.

## Tabu search (week 3, TSP · local search)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-tabu.html

Tabu search always moves, even downhill, to escape local optima. To avoid simply stepping back to where it came from, it keeps a short-term memory of recent moves that are forbidden (tabu) for a few iterations.

Definition: At each iteration, move to the best neighbour whose move is not tabu. Mark that move tabu for tt iterations (the tenure). A tabu move is allowed anyway if it gives a tour better than any seen (aspiration; the studio can switch it off to show the difference). Return the best tour seen.

Pseudocode:

```
N ← start;  bestSeen ← N
repeat for k iterations
    candidates ← MoveGen(N), best first
    pick the first candidate that is not tabu,
         or is tabu but better than bestSeen (aspiration)
    make its key tabu for tt iterations
    N ← candidate;  if N better than bestSeen: bestSeen ← N
return bestSeen
```

- tabu(m) ⇔ t_used < t ≤ t_used + tt: a move stays forbidden for tt iterations. Short tenure risks cycling; long tenure can block good moves.
- aspiration: allow m if cost(m(N)) < cost(bestSeen): a forbidden move is fine if it finds a new best. Tabu exists to stop cycling, not to block real improvements.

Memory turns a greedy walk into a systematic one. On small instances a short tenure leads to cycles; a frequency memory (prefer rarely-used moves) further diversifies the search.

Complete: no. Optimal: no. Time: iterations × |N|. Space: O(tt).

- Trap: Tabu takes the best non-tabu move even if it is worse than the current tour.
- Trap: Apply aspiration before rejecting a tabu move. Seven cities (tabu aspiration) in the examples: in iteration 4 swap D↔F is still tabu from iteration 1, but it gives 241 < bestSeen 249, so it is taken and reaches the optimum; with aspiration off the best found is only 249.
- Trap: Return bestSeen, not the final current tour.
- Trap: The tenure matters: on Six cities in 8 iterations, tenure 2 lands on an already visited tour 5 times (short memory, cycling), tenure 3 only 3 times and it explores tours costing 237 and 233 on the way.

## Iterated hill climbing (week 3, TSP · local search)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-ihc.html

If one hill climb gets stuck, start again from somewhere else. Iterated hill climbing repeats hill climbing from random starting tours and keeps the best local optimum found.

Definition: Repeat r times: generate a random tour, hill climb to a local optimum, remember it if it is the best so far.

Pseudocode:

```
best ← none
repeat r times
    N ← random tour
    N ← HillClimbing(N)
    if N better than best: best ← N
return best
```

- P(success) ≈ 1 − (1 − p)^r: with r restarts, each landing in the optimum's basin with probability p. More restarts make it more likely that at least one starts in the right basin.

Simple and effective when local optima are many but hill climbing is cheap. It wastes effort if most random starts lead to the same poor basin.

Complete: no. Optimal: no. Time: r × hill climb. Space: O(n).

- Trap: Each restart is independent: nothing is learned between restarts.
- Trap: Random starts are usually much worse than constructive tours.
- Trap: Different starts end in different local optima: on Six cities with 5 restarts the optima are 229, 224, 224, 229, 224, so one climb can be stuck at 229 while another finds 224.

## Best neighbour, k moves (week 3, TSP · local search)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-best-neighbour-moves.html

Hill climbing stops when no neighbour is better. A tempting fix is to keep going: always move to the best neighbour, even if it is worse. With no memory, this does not escape for long. From a local optimum the best neighbour is worse, but from there the best neighbour is usually the local optimum again, so the search bounces back and forth.

Definition: Repeat a fixed number k of times: generate all neighbours of the current tour with the chosen MoveGen and move to the cheapest one (ties alphabetically by tour). There is no test for improvement and no memory of visited tours.

Pseudocode:

```
N ← start;  bestSeen ← N
repeat k moves
    N ← the best neighbour of N          # lowest cost, even if worse than N
    if N better than bestSeen: bestSeen ← N
    if N was visited before: report the cycle
return bestSeen
```

- cycle length = move now − move when this tour was first visited: how many moves until the tour returns. A deterministic rule applied to a state we already visited must reproduce the same path again.

It shows why local search needs more than a greedy best-neighbour rule: tabu search adds a memory (forbidden moves) and simulated annealing adds randomness precisely to break this cycle.

Complete: no. Optimal: no. Time: k scans of the neighbourhood. Space: O(n).

- Trap: Reporting the final tour instead of the best tour seen.
- Trap: Thinking that moving uphill alone is enough to escape a local optimum: without memory or randomness it goes straight back. On Six cities the walk bounces between 224 and 229 for ever (a cycle of length 2 from move 1), exactly the repetition that tabu search's memory forbids.

## Random walk (week 3, TSP · local search)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-random-walk.html

A random walk is the opposite extreme of hill climbing: it ignores costs entirely and steps to a random neighbour each time. It is a baseline that shows how much the evaluation function helps.

Definition: From the current tour move to a uniformly random neighbour; record the best tour seen.

Pseudocode:

```
N ← start;  bestSeen ← N
repeat k times
    N ← random neighbour of N
    if N better than bestSeen: bestSeen ← N
return bestSeen
```

- P(next = X) = 1 / |N(current)|: every neighbour is equally likely. No bias toward better tours, so the walk drifts toward wherever most tours are: mostly bad ones.

Pure exploration can in principle reach anything, but without guidance it rarely finds good tours in reasonable time.

Complete: no. Optimal: no. Time: k samples. Space: O(n).

- Trap: Simulated annealing at very high temperature behaves almost like this (a coin flip per move).
- Trap: Do not expect it to settle: on Six cities started from the Greedy tour (238) the cost jumps up and down by tens of units from step to step with no downward trend (more steps give a range of roughly 220 to 380), and the last step reports that range. Only the remembered bestSeen is useful.

## Simulated annealing (week 3, TSP · local search)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-sa.html

Simulated annealing borrows from metalworking: hot metal moves freely, then settles into a strong structure as it cools. The search accepts worse moves often while the 'temperature' is high, and becomes stricter as it cools.

Definition: Pick a random neighbour X of the current tour N. Compute ΔE = cost(N) − cost(X) (positive means X is better) and move with probability P = 1/(1 + e^(−ΔE/T)). Lower T after each step.

Pseudocode:

```
N ← start;  bestSeen ← N;  T ← T0
repeat k times
    X ← random neighbour of N
    ΔE ← cost(N) − cost(X)            # positive = improvement
    P ← 1 / (1 + e^(−ΔE / T))
    if random u < P: N ← X
    if N better than bestSeen: bestSeen ← N
    T ← α · T
return bestSeen
```

- P = 1 / (1 + e^(−ΔE/T)): a sigmoid of ΔE scaled by temperature. ΔE > 0 gives P > ½, ΔE < 0 gives P < ½; larger |ΔE| pushes P toward 1 or 0.
- T → ∞: P → ½;   T → 0: P → 1 if ΔE > 0, 0 if ΔE < 0: hot = coin flip, cold = hill climbing. Temperature controls the balance between exploration and exploitation.
- Tₖ = T₀ · αᵏ: temperature after k steps. Slow cooling (α close to 1) gives more time to escape local optima.

Accepting some worse moves lets SA leave local optima; cooling makes it settle. With this sigmoid rule even a better move can be rejected (P < 1), so always keep the best tour seen.

Complete: no. Optimal: no guarantee in practice (only in the limit of extremely slow cooling). Time: k samples. Space: O(n).

- Trap: ΔE sign: define it so that positive means better for the problem at hand.
- Trap: With the sigmoid rule, P(better move) < 1 at finite T.
- Trap: Return bestSeen: the current tour can wander off the best one.
- Trap: Temperature is the whole story: on Six cities with the default settings worse moves are accepted at k = 1 (T = 30) and k = 7 (T = 11); at k = 12 (T = 5) only an improving move is taken, and the run escapes the 229 trap to reach 224. Try T0 = 1: the sigmoid is so steep that it behaves like hill climbing and stays at 229.

## Best First on a state space (week 3, Graph search · informed)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/statespace-best-first.html

Best First Search trusts the heuristic completely. In the 8-puzzle, h counts tiles out of place or their Manhattan distance to the goal squares; the board that looks nearest to the goal is expanded first.

Definition: OPEN holds node pairs (state, parent, h) ordered by h. The goal test is on picking from OPEN, ties break alphabetically (by state), and a state already on OPEN or CLOSED is not added again. Unlike A*, the cost already paid is ignored.

Pseudocode:

```
OPEN ← [(S, nil, h(S))];  CLOSED ← [ ]
while OPEN not empty
    N ← the pair with the least h;  remove it      # ties: alphabetical
    if GoalTest(N): return the path
    CLOSED ← N : CLOSED
    children ← MoveGen(N) minus states on OPEN or CLOSED
    OPEN ← OPEN ++ children, sorted by h
```

- tiles out of place: h₁ = number of tiles not on their goal square: blank not counted. Each such tile needs at least one move.
- Manhattan: h₂ = Σ |row − goal row| + |col − goal col|: sum of tile distances. A tile moves one square per move, so it needs at least its Manhattan distance; h₂ ≥ h₁.

Both heuristics are admissible for the 8-puzzle, but Best First ignores g, so it may take a long way round. Compare the length of its solution with A*'s on the same board.

Complete: yes on a finite space with CLOSED. Optimal: no. Time: exponential worst case. Space: exponential worst case.

- Trap: Best First is not optimal even with an admissible h: on example space-8-puzzle-12 it returns a 44-move solution with tiles out of place (the shortest has 12). With Manhattan distance it happens to find 12 moves there, which is luck, not a guarantee.
- Trap: A heuristic that is 0 everywhere turns the order into ties, i.e. alphabetical order of states.
- Trap: For water jugs there is no useful h (it is 0); for missionaries and cannibals the studio uses the full-boat crossing bound.

## Iterated hill climbing (week 4, SAT · stochastic)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/sat-ihc.html

One hill climb ends at the first local maximum it meets, and which one it meets depends on where it started. Iterated hill climbing runs the same N1 hill climb from several starting assignments and keeps the best. It is the simplest way of adding randomness to local search.

Definition: Choose r starting bit strings (random, or listed explicitly). From each run strict N1 hill climbing (best one-flip neighbour, ties to the lowest bit, move only if h strictly increases). Remember the string with the largest h. Stop early if some run reaches h = m.

Pseudocode:

```
best ← none
for each start S (given, or r random bit strings)
    N ← HillClimbing_N1(S)
    if h(N) > h(best): best ← N
    if h(best) = m: stop (solved)
return best
```

- P(at least one start reaches the solution) = 1 − (1 − q)^r: q = fraction of starts whose hill climb ends at the solution. Starts are independent, so all r fail with probability (1 − q)^r. **Supplementary** (not in the course notes).

On the four-variable course example hill climbing from 0000 stops at 1000 (h 5). Among five starts only 0101 climbs on to 1101 (h 6). More starts means more chances, but each start is a fresh gamble: nothing learned in one run is used in the next.

Complete: no. Optimal: no. Time: r hill climbs. Space: O(n).

- Trap: Restarts are independent: iterated hill climbing does not remember where earlier runs failed.
- Trap: Two different starts can end in the same local maximum, so r starts do not give r different answers (on sat-four-var the starts 1110 and 0010 both climb to 1010).
- Trap: Failing on all r starts does not prove the formula unsatisfiable.

## Stochastic hill climbing (fixed T) (week 4, SAT · stochastic)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/sat-stochastic-hc.html

Stochastic hill climbing keeps the idea of preferring uphill moves but replaces the hard rule 'only if better' by a probability. A better neighbour is accepted with probability above one half, a worse one with probability below one half, and the temperature T decides how sharp that preference is. T stays fixed; simulated annealing is the version that lowers it.

Definition: Choose a random neighbour X of N. Let ΔE = h(X) − h(N); for SAT we maximise h, so ΔE > 0 is an improvement. Accept X with probability P = 1/(1 + e^(−ΔE/T)); draw u uniformly in [0, 1) and move if u < P.

Pseudocode:

```
N ← start;  bestSeen ← N
repeat k times
    X ← random neighbour of N (flip a random bit)
    ΔE ← h(X) − h(N)                  # positive = improvement (we maximise h)
    P ← 1 / (1 + e^(−ΔE / T))
    if random u < P: N ← X
    if h(N) > h(bestSeen): bestSeen ← N
return bestSeen
```

- P = 1 / (1 + e^(−ΔE/T)): a sigmoid in ΔE/T. ΔE = 0 gives exactly ½; ΔE > 0 gives more than ½ and ΔE < 0 less than ½, approaching 1 and 0 as |ΔE|/T grows.
- T → 0: hill climbing;   T → ∞: random walk: the two extremes. Small T makes the sigmoid a step at ΔE = 0 (only improving moves); large T flattens it to ½ (a coin flip, i.e. random walk).

A worse neighbour can still be accepted, so the search can walk down off a local maximum such as 1000 (h 5) towards 1101 (h 6). Because T never falls, it keeps wandering even after it has found a good string, which is why we report bestSeen.

Complete: no. Optimal: no. Time: k samples. Space: O(n).

- Trap: With the sigmoid rule even an improving move can be rejected (P < 1 at finite T).
- Trap: ΔE is h(new) − h(current) here: do not copy the TSP sign.
- Trap: Fixed T is a compromise: too hot is a random walk (try T = 100), too cold is hill climbing (try T = 0.05). Annealing varies it.

## Simulated annealing (week 4, SAT · stochastic)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/sat-sa.html

Simulated annealing borrows from metalworking: hot metal moves freely, then settles as it cools. The search accepts worse moves often while the temperature is high and becomes stricter as it cools, so it explores first and exploits later.

Definition: Pick a random one-flip neighbour X of N. Compute ΔE = h(X) − h(N) (positive means X satisfies more clauses) and move with probability P = 1/(1 + e^(−ΔE/T)). After every step lower T according to the cooling schedule. Return the best string seen.

Pseudocode:

```
N ← start;  bestSeen ← N;  T ← T0
repeat k times
    X ← N with a random bit flipped
    ΔE ← h(X) − h(N)                  # positive = improvement (we maximise h)
    P ← 1 / (1 + e^(−ΔE / T))
    if random u < P: N ← X
    if h(N) > h(bestSeen): bestSeen ← N
    T ← next temperature (geometric: α·T, or linear down to Tend)
return bestSeen
```

- P = 1 / (1 + e^(−ΔE/T)): a sigmoid of ΔE scaled by temperature. ΔE > 0 gives P > ½, ΔE < 0 gives P < ½; larger |ΔE|/T pushes P toward 1 or 0.
- T → ∞: P → ½;   T → 0: P → 1 if ΔE > 0, 0 if ΔE < 0: hot = coin flip, cold = hill climbing. Temperature sets the balance between exploration and exploitation.
- Tₖ = T₀ · αᵏ: geometric cooling after k steps. Slow cooling (α close to 1) leaves more time to escape local maxima.
- Tₖ = T₀ − k · (T₀ − Tend)/steps: linear cooling. **Supplementary**: an alternative schedule, not in the course notes; it reaches Tend exactly at the last step.

Accepting some worse moves lets the search leave a local maximum such as 1000 (h 5) and cooling makes it settle near a good string. With the sigmoid rule even an improving move can be rejected, so always keep bestSeen. Compare with the random walk, which ignores h: on sat-ten-var (10 variables, 3 solutions among 1024) 30 steps solve it for 51 of 100 seeds with annealing and 7 of 100 with the random walk; seed 2 shows it (annealing solves it, the walk reaches only h 46 of 48). Raise T0 a lot and annealing degrades towards the random walk, lower it and it behaves like hill climbing.

Complete: no. Optimal: only with impractically slow cooling. Time: k samples. Space: O(n).

- Trap: ΔE sign: for SAT it is h(new) − h(current), the reverse of the TSP cost version.
- Trap: At finite T an improving move is still rejected with probability 1 − P.
- Trap: Return bestSeen: the current string may wander off the best one.
- Trap: Results depend on the seed; the same seed repeats the run exactly.

## Genetic algorithm (week 4, SAT · genetic)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/sat-ga.html

A genetic algorithm keeps a whole population of candidate assignments instead of a single one. Fitter strings (more clauses satisfied) are more likely to become parents; crossover mixes the bits of two parents and mutation occasionally flips a bit, which can create strings that neither parent could.

Definition: Fitness of a string is h, the number of satisfied clauses. Selection probability is p = h / Σh (roulette wheel: the cumulative probabilities partition [0, 1) and a uniform u picks the interval it falls in). Pairs of selected parents are crossed at a random one-point cut, and each child is mutated with probability pm by flipping one random bit.

Pseudocode:

```
Pop ← N bit strings (given, or random)
repeat for g generations
    fitness(x) ← h(x);   p(x) ← h(x) / Σ h
    pool ← N strings drawn by roulette-wheel (spin u, take the first x with cumulative p ≥ u)
    for each consecutive pair (a, b) of the pool
        cut ← random point in 1..n−1;   children ← a[0..cut)+b[cut..), b[0..cut)+a[cut..)
        with probability pm flip one random bit of each child
    Pop ← the children
return the best string ever seen
```

- p(xᵢ) = h(xᵢ) / Σⱼ h(xⱼ): selection probability proportional to fitness. The probabilities sum to 1, and a string with twice the fitness gets twice the share of the wheel.
- cumulative cᵢ = p(x₁) + … + p(xᵢ): the wheel's boundaries. u falls in the interval (cᵢ₋₁, cᵢ] of exactly one member, so the draw has the right probabilities.

Crossover recombines good partial assignments, mutation keeps diversity. On the course example a single generation can produce the solution 1101 when mutation flips the right bit of a child that is one flip away from it. The method is incomplete: with few generations or a tiny population it may never find a solution.

Complete: no. Optimal: no. Time: N·g evaluations. Space: O(N·n).

- Trap: Crossover only recombines bit values already present in the population; only mutation creates new ones. Default population 1000,0110,0011,1100, 1 generation: with pm = 0.5 and seed 9 the solution 1101 is made by mutation (child 1100 mutated at d); with pm = 0 and seed 1 it is made by crossover alone (1100 × 0011 cut after c gives 1101). With the population 1000,0110,1100,0100, where every string has d = 0, pm = 0 can never produce 1101 however many generations you run, while pm = 0.5 usually finds it.
- Trap: Fitness-proportional selection is weak when all h values are close: the probabilities are then almost equal.
- Trap: If every h is 0 the wheel would divide by zero; the trace falls back to uniform probabilities.
- Trap: A solution found in a child must be recorded when it appears: the next generation may lose it.
- Trap: Results depend on the seed and on the initial population; the same inputs repeat the run exactly.

## Stochastic hill climbing (week 4, TSP · local search)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-stochastic-hc.html

Ordinary hill climbing only ever accepts improvements and so gets stuck at the first local optimum. Stochastic hill climbing keeps the 'look at one random neighbour' step but accepts it with a probability that depends on how much better or worse it is, so it can sometimes walk downhill and escape.

Definition: At a fixed temperature T, move from N to a random neighbour X with probability P = 1/(1 + e^(−ΔE/T)), where ΔE = cost(N) − cost(X) (positive means X is shorter). Unlike simulated annealing, T never changes.

Pseudocode:

```
N ← start;  bestSeen ← N
repeat k times
    X ← random neighbour of N
    ΔE ← cost(N) − cost(X)            # positive = improvement
    P ← 1 / (1 + e^(−ΔE / T))         # T is fixed
    if random u < P: N ← X
    if N better than bestSeen: bestSeen ← N
return bestSeen
```

- P = 1 / (1 + e^(−ΔE/T)): sigmoid of ΔE/T. ΔE > 0 gives P > ½, ΔE < 0 gives P < ½, ΔE = 0 gives P = ½ whatever T is.
- T large: P → ½;   T small: P → 1 (ΔE>0) or 0 (ΔE<0): hot is a coin flip, cold is hill climbing. T scales ΔE: dividing by a big T squashes all differences; a small T amplifies them.

A fixed T is a fixed compromise: too hot and the search wanders at random, too cold and it behaves like plain hill climbing and stalls in a local optimum. Annealing resolves this by lowering T over time.

Complete: no. Optimal: no. Time: k samples. Space: O(n).

- Trap: ΔE is cost(current) − cost(next): improvement positive, the opposite of some textbooks.
- Trap: Even an improving move is only accepted with probability P < 1 at finite T, so keep the best tour seen.
- Trap: The same seed gives the same run; change the seed, not the code, to see a different one.

## Genetic algorithm (week 4, TSP · genetic)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-ga.html

A genetic algorithm evolves a population of tours. Better tours are more likely to be chosen as parents, parents are combined by crossover, children are occasionally mutated, and the population slowly improves.

Definition: Repeat for g generations: compute fitness, select N parents by roulette wheel (probability proportional to fitness), cross pairs, mutate with a small probability, and replace the weakest members with the strongest offspring.

Pseudocode:

```
P ← N random tours
repeat for g generations
    fitness(x) ← K / cost(x)
    S ← N roulette-wheel spins over P         (probability ∝ fitness)
    pair S as (1,2), (3,4), …; crossover each pair → offspring
    with probability pm mutate an offspring (swap two cities)
    replace the k weakest of P with the k strongest offspring
return best member of P
```

- pᵢ = fᵢ / Σⱼ fⱼ,   fᵢ = K / costᵢ: share of the wheel for member i. Fitter members get bigger slices, but every member keeps some chance.
- angleᵢ = 360° · pᵢ;   pick i if cumᵢ₋₁ < u ≤ cumᵢ: spin u in [0,1) and see which slice it lands in. This is how the course traces roulette selection by hand.

Selection pushes toward good tours, crossover mixes their good parts, and mutation keeps exploring. Too much selection pressure makes the population identical too soon (premature convergence).

Complete: no. Optimal: no. Time: O(g · N · n). Space: O(N · n).

- Trap: Fitness must be inverted for a minimisation problem.
- Trap: If the population converges early: raise mutation, lower selection pressure, enlarge the population. Nine cities (GA premature convergence) in the examples: with Generations 30, Replace k 3 and mutation 0 the whole population becomes one tour costing 329 (optimum 255); with mutation 0.9 the same run reaches 255. Watch the distinct tours counter.
- Trap: Cumulative probabilities decide roulette picks; recompute them carefully.

## Crossover lab (week 4, TSP · genetic)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-crossover-lab.html

Genetic algorithms combine two good tours into a child. For the TSP that is tricky: cutting two city lists and gluing the halves usually repeats some cities and loses others. TSP crossovers are designed to always produce valid tours.

Definition: A crossover takes parent tours P1, P2 and builds a child that inherits structure from both: positions (cycle crossover), a segment plus positions (PMX), a segment plus relative order (order crossover), edges (alternating edges, heuristic crossover), or a prefix in ordinal code (ordinal crossover).

Pseudocode:

```
CX:  follow P1[i] → city P2[i] → its position in P1 …; odd cycles from P1, even from P2
```
