```
PMX: copy P1[a..b]; elsewhere take P2's city, following the a..b mapping while it is taken
OX:  copy P1[a..b]; fill the blanks left to right with P2's order minus those cities
AEX: next city from P1, then P2, then P1 …; on a cycle use the other parent, else first unvisited
HX:  from each city take the shorter of the two parents' next edges
Ordinal: encode each tour by indices into the shrinking city list; single-point crossover; decode
```

- ordinal gene i ∈ {1, …, n−i+1}: the i-th index points into the n−i+1 cities still unvisited. Any mix of two such sequences is still a legal sequence, so single-point crossover is always valid.
- adjacency: a[X] = city after X: store who comes next instead of the order. Tour cost depends on edges, so operators that pass on edges pass on the useful information.

Each operator preserves a different property of the parents. Since cost depends on edges, edge- and order-preserving operators usually produce better children than position-preserving ones.

Complete: n/a. Optimal: n/a. Time: O(n) to O(n²) per child. Space: O(n).

- Trap: Know the exact fill convention for OX in your course (left to right here).
- Trap: PMX: keep following the mapping chain until the city is not already placed.
- Trap: Naive single-point crossover on paths is invalid in general.

## Representation lab (week 4, TSP · genetic)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-representation-lab.html

A genetic algorithm needs a way to write a tour as a string it can cut and recombine. The same tour can be written as the path (visit order), as an adjacency list (who follows whom) or as an ordinal string (index into a shrinking list). Each representation allows different crossover operators and has different pitfalls.

Definition: Path: the cities in visiting order. Adjacency: entry i is the city that follows the i-th city (alphabetical order) in the tour. Ordinal: with a reference list of the tour's cities in alphabetical order, gene 1 is the position of the first tour city in that list; delete it; gene 2 is the position of the second tour city in the remaining list; and so on.

Pseudocode:

```
Ordinal encode:  ref ← the cities of the tour in alphabetical order
    for each city c of the tour, in order:  gene ← position of c in ref (1-based);  delete c from ref
Ordinal decode:  ref ← same list;  for each gene g: city ← g-th city of ref;  delete it from ref
Adjacency encode: a[c] ← the city after c in the tour (cyclic), listed in alphabetical order of c
Adjacency decode: start at the first city, repeatedly go to a[current]; valid iff all n cities are visited before returning
Crossover: cut two ordinal strings after k genes and swap the tails; decode both children
```

- gene i ∈ {1, …, n−i+1}: the i-th gene indexes a list that already lost i−1 cities. Mixing the first genes of one string with the later genes of another never leaves this range, so decoding cannot fail.
- a[c] = successor of c: adjacency stores edges, directed along the tour. A list is a tour only if following a[ ] from any city visits all n cities before returning; two or more separate cycles are legal lists but not tours.
- a_reverse = a⁻¹: the reversed tour's adjacency is the inverse permutation. A tour and its reverse are the same cycle with the same cost, so both lists are valid representations.

Ordinal representation is the course's example of a representation chosen so that a plain one-point crossover is legal. The price is that gene positions mean different things depending on earlier genes, so a child can look unlike either parent.

Complete: n/a. Optimal: n/a. Time: O(n²). Space: O(n).

- Trap: The reference list is the tour's own cities in alphabetical order, not the order of the tour.
- Trap: Genes count from 1, and the list shrinks after every deletion.
- Trap: Adjacency is read in alphabetical order of the city, not along the tour.
- Trap: A valid-looking adjacency list can break into sub-cycles; check that it is one cycle through every city.

## Ant colony optimisation (week 4, TSP · swarm)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-aco.html

Real ants find short paths by leaving pheromone: short routes are travelled more often, collect more pheromone, and attract more ants. Ant colony optimisation copies this with artificial ants building tours on a pheromone map.

Definition: Each ant builds a tour, choosing the next city j from i with probability proportional to τᵢⱼ^α · (1/dᵢⱼ)^β. After all ants finish, pheromone evaporates by a factor (1−ρ) and each ant adds Q/L on the edges of its tour.

Pseudocode:

```
τ ← τ0 on every edge;  bestTour ← nil
repeat for t iterations
    place m ants on cities
    each ant: repeat n−1 times
        choose next j with P(i→j) = τij^α ηij^β / Σ τih^α ηih^β,  η = 1/d
    update bestTour
    τ ← (1 − ρ) τ                         # evaporation
    for each ant, for each edge of its tour: τ += Q / L(ant)
return bestTour
```

- P(i→j) = τᵢⱼ^α ηᵢⱼ^β / Σ over unvisited h of τᵢₕ^α ηᵢₕ^β,   η = 1/d: pheromone strength times visibility, normalised. α weighs learned experience, β weighs the greedy distance heuristic.
- τᵢⱼ ← (1 − ρ) τᵢⱼ + Σₖ Q / Lₖ: evaporate, then deposit in proportion to tour quality. Edges shared by many short tours grow; unused edges fade.

Combines a greedy heuristic with experience shared through the environment. Large α can lock in early choices; large ρ forgets quickly and keeps exploring.

Complete: no. Optimal: no. Time: O(m · n²) per iteration. Space: O(n²).

- Trap: Normalise only over unvisited cities.
- Trap: Evaporate before depositing (course order).
- Trap: β = 0 ignores distance; α = 0 ignores pheromone and gives a randomised nearest neighbour.
- Trap: Reinforcement is visible in the update steps: on Six cities the pheromone on the six strongest edges rises from about 60% to about 70% of the total within a few iterations (40% if spread evenly), while unused edges evaporate. A larger ρ forgets faster.

## Branch & bound (exact) (week 5, TSP · exact)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/tsp-branch-and-bound.html

Brute force looks at every tour. Branch and bound looks at families of tours: a node stands for 'every tour that contains these edges and avoids those edges', and a cheap lower bound says how good any tour in the family could possibly be. If even the optimistic bound cannot beat the best tour already found, the whole family is discarded unseen.

Definition: A node is a pair (included edges, excluded edges). Its lower bound is ½ Σ over cities of the cost of the two cheapest admissible edges at that city: every tour uses exactly two edges at each city, and each edge is counted from both ends, hence the half. Branching picks an undecided edge e and creates two children: include e and exclude e. A node is a complete tour when every city has two included edges.

Pseudocode:

```
best ← ∞ (or the cost of a known tour);  OPEN ← [root: no edge decided]
while OPEN is not empty
    N ← pick a node from OPEN                       # DFS: newest;  best-first: lowest bound
    LB(N) ← ½ · Σ over cities of the two cheapest admissible edges
             (included edges first; excluded edges, edges at a city that already has 2 included
              edges, and edges closing a short cycle are not admissible)
    if LB(N) ≥ best: prune N
    else if every city has 2 included edges: best ← cost (a complete tour)
    else  e ← cheapest undecided edge in the bound
          children: N + include e,  N + exclude e   (drop infeasible ones)
return best
```

- LB = ½ Σ_c (e₁(c) + e₂(c)): half the sum over cities of the two cheapest admissible edges at c. Any tour has two edges at each city and each edge touches two cities, so its cost is half the sum of those per-city costs; choosing the cheapest two at every city can only lower that sum.
- prune if LB ≥ best: the optimistic cost is not below the incumbent. No tour in this family can be strictly better than the best tour already found.

The bound costs O(n²) per node but can remove huge subtrees. It is tight when the cheap edges at each city fit together into one tour, and weak when they do not, which is why the order in which edges are decided and a good first tour matter.

Complete: yes. Optimal: yes. Time: O(n!) worst case. Space: O(n) per node, DFS.

- Trap: The bound is half the sum, not the sum.
- Trap: An included edge counts for both of its cities; a city with two included edges contributes exactly those two.
- Trap: An edge at a city that already has two included edges is not admissible for its other end either.
- Trap: A bound can be a fraction (x.5); compare it with integer tour costs without rounding.
- Trap: Pruning depends on the best tour found so far. On Six cities depth-first picks 68 nodes, finds five successively better tours (238, 237, 233, 229, 224) and prunes 24 subtrees; best-first picks 49 nodes and finds only the optimum; depth-first with Initial best 229 picks 55. The Initial best must be above the optimum: below it no tour is found.

## Uniform Cost Search (week 5, Graph search · optimal)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-ucs.html

Uniform Cost Search always expands the cheapest path found so far. With different edge costs it finds the cheapest route, not just the one with the fewest steps.

Definition: A state-space search problem has a start node S, a goal test, and a MoveGen function that lists the neighbours of a node. The search keeps two lists: OPEN (nodes generated but not yet expanded) and CLOSED (nodes already expanded). Each entry is a node pair (node, parent, value) so the path can be read back through parents. OPEN is ordered by g(N), the cost from S to N. If a cheaper path to a node already seen is found, its parent and g are updated.

Pseudocode:

```
OPEN ← [(S, nil, 0)] ordered by g
while OPEN not empty
    N ← node with least g;  remove it
    if GoalTest(N): return the path
    move N to CLOSED
    for each child C of N with g' = g(N) + k(N,C)
        new: add (C, N, g') to OPEN
        on OPEN/CLOSED with larger g: update parent and g (reopen if on CLOSED)
```

- g(C) = g(N) + k(N, C): cost so far plus the edge. Paths are extended one edge at a time.
- pick argmin g on OPEN: cheapest frontier node first. With non-negative costs this expands nodes in order of their true distance from S.

Optimal for non-negative edge costs; it is Dijkstra's algorithm stopped at the goal. It explores in all directions because it has no idea where the goal is.

Complete: yes. Optimal: yes. Time: O(b^(1+C*/ε)). Space: same.

- Trap: Apply the goal test when the goal is removed from OPEN, not when it is generated.
- Trap: Remember to update g and the parent on cheaper paths: in 'Dijkstra demo' G is first reached at 9 (via C) and then improved to 8 (via D); keeping the first path would give a wrong answer.
- Trap: UCS ignores the goal's direction: it expands every node cheaper than the optimum (compare the expansions of A* on the 'Weighted graph' example: 8 for UCS, 5 for A*).

## Dijkstra's Algorithm (week 5, Graph search · optimal)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-dijkstra.html

Dijkstra's algorithm is Uniform Cost Search written as a table. Each node carries a best-known distance d. The WHITE node with the smallest d is made BLACK, and then its neighbours are checked to see whether going through it gives them a shorter distance.

Definition: Colour every node WHITE and give it d = ∞, except the start with d = 0. Pick the WHITE node N with least d and colour it BLACK: its d is now the true shortest distance from the start. For each WHITE neighbour C of N with edge cost k, if d(N)+k < d(C) then set d(C) = d(N)+k and parent(C) = N (a relaxation). Stop when the goal is coloured BLACK, then follow the parents back to the start.

Pseudocode:

```
d(S) ← 0;  d(v) ← ∞ for the rest;  all nodes WHITE
repeat
    N ← WHITE node with least d(N)           # ties: alphabetical
    colour N BLACK
    if N = goal: return the path (follow parents)
    for each WHITE neighbour C of N with edge cost k:
        if d(N) + k < d(C):                  # relaxation
            d(C) ← d(N) + k;  parent(C) ← N
until no WHITE node has d < ∞              # goal unreachable
```

- d(N) + k(N,C) < d(C)  ⇒  d(C) ← d(N) + k(N,C): relaxation. A shorter way to C through the newly final node N has been found, so C's estimate improves.
- pick argmin d over WHITE nodes: closest unfinished node. With non-negative costs no later path can reach it more cheaply, so it can be made BLACK.

It gives the shortest path to every node it blackens, and to the goal once the goal is picked. It is the same search as UCS: OPEN is the set of WHITE nodes with finite d, CLOSED is the BLACK set. It has no sense of direction, so it spreads in all directions.

Complete: yes (finite graph). Optimal: yes (non-negative costs). Time: O(V²) or O(E log V). Space: O(V).

- Trap: Only WHITE neighbours are relaxed: a BLACK node is already final.
- Trap: Edge costs must not be negative; with negative edges a BLACK node could still improve.
- Trap: d of a node can change several times before it turns BLACK (for example G falling from 9 to 8): only the BLACK value is final.
- Trap: Count picks, not relaxations.

## Branch & Bound (state space) (week 5, Graph search · optimal)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-branch-and-bound.html

Branch & Bound explores a tree of paths, always refining the cheapest partial path. Nothing records which states have already been reached, so the same state can be generated again by a different path. This tracer shows how often each state occurs in the search tree.

Definition: Each OPEN entry is one partial path from S, stored as a node pair (node, parent, g). A refinement takes the cheapest entry and replaces it by its children, one per neighbour that is not already on that path (so a path never loops). There is no CLOSED list, so two different paths to the same state are both kept as separate tree nodes. The goal test is applied when the goal is picked from OPEN; its g is then the cost of the cheapest path, because every other entry on OPEN costs at least as much.

Pseudocode:

```
OPEN ← [(S, nil, g=0)]                      # a search TREE: no CLOSED list
repeat
    N ← node on OPEN with least g                # ties: alphabetical, then oldest
    remove N from OPEN;  count one refinement
    if GoalTest(N): return the path of N         # g(N) is the bound: nothing on OPEN is cheaper
    for each child C of N not already on N's own path
        add (C, N, g(N)+k(N,C)) to OPEN          # even if C already occurs elsewhere in the tree
```

- g(C) = g(N) + k(N, C): cost of the extended path. Each tree node carries the cost of its own path.
- tree size = Σ occurrences(state): every path prefix is a node. Without CLOSED, merging never happens, so the tree can be much larger than the graph.

It finds the optimal path like UCS, but because it does not merge duplicates it does more work. Adding a CLOSED list (and updating g on cheaper paths) turns it into Dijkstra's algorithm. The occurrence counts show exactly what a CLOSED list saves.

Complete: yes (finite graph, no loops on a path). Optimal: yes (non-negative costs). Time: exponential in the worst case. Space: all tree nodes.

- Trap: Duplicates: on 'Graph T' A appears twice, B twice and G three times, while Dijkstra on the same graph closes each node once; on the 4×5 grid the tree has hundreds of nodes for 20 states.
- Trap: The goal state may itself appear several times in the tree; only the first one picked ends the search.
- Trap: Do not stop when the goal is generated: stop when it is picked.
- Trap: A pick of a node is counted as a refinement even when it is the goal.

## British Museum (brute force on paths) (week 5, Graph search · optimal)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-british-museum.html

The British Museum method looks at every possible path, one by one, and keeps the cheapest. It needs no cleverness and no heuristic, and its answer is the optimum. Its cost is the number of paths, which explodes as the graph grows.

Definition: Enumerate all simple paths (no repeated node) from S to the goal by depth-first exploration, in alphabetical order of neighbours. Each time a path reaches the goal, compare its cost with the best so far and keep the cheaper (the earlier one is kept on a tie). The answer has the same cost as Uniform Cost Search. The tracer shows each complete path found; after the first 40 it only reports improvements, and it counts everything.

Pseudocode:

```
best ← none;  cost* ← ∞
DFS over simple paths from S (a node may not repeat on the current path):
    if the path ends at the goal:
        if cost(path) < cost*: best ← path;  cost* ← cost(path)
        (do not extend a path past the goal)
return best
```

- cost(path) = Σ k(edge): sum of edge costs. Paths are compared by total cost.
- answer = min over all simple S→goal paths: exhaustive minimum. Nothing is skipped, so the minimum is the true optimum.

It shows how much work the intelligent methods avoid. Uniform Cost Search finds the same cost while looking at a tiny fraction of the paths.

Complete: yes. Optimal: yes. Time: exponential (number of simple paths). Space: O(path length).

- Trap: The number of simple paths can be exponential in the number of nodes.
- Trap: It must not reuse a node on the same path, otherwise cycles give infinitely many paths.
- Trap: Finding the first path is not enough: all paths must be tried.

## A* (week 5, Graph search · optimal)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-astar.html

A* combines the cost already paid with an estimate of the cost remaining. With an estimate that never overestimates, it finds the cheapest path and usually expands far fewer nodes than Uniform Cost Search.

Definition: A state-space search problem has a start node S, a goal test, and a MoveGen function that lists the neighbours of a node. The search keeps two lists: OPEN (nodes generated but not yet expanded) and CLOSED (nodes already expanded). Each entry is a node pair (node, parent, value) so the path can be read back through parents. OPEN is ordered by f(N) = g(N) + w·h(N). With w = 1 and an admissible h this is A*; with w > 1 it is weighted A*.

Pseudocode:

```
OPEN ← [(S, nil, g=0)] ordered by f = g + w·h
while OPEN not empty
    N ← node with least f;  remove it
    if GoalTest(N): return the path
    move N to CLOSED
    for each child C with g' = g(N) + k(N,C)
        new: add to OPEN
        cheaper than its pair on OPEN/CLOSED: update parent and g (reopen if CLOSED)
```

- f(N) = g(N) + h(N): paid so far plus estimated remainder. Balances progress (g) against promise (h).
- admissible: h(N) ≤ h*(N) for all N: never overestimate the true remaining cost. Then f never overestimates the true cost of a path through N, so the optimal path is never skipped.
- consistent: h(N) ≤ k(N,M) + h(M): the triangle inequality for h. Then f never decreases along a path and closed nodes never need reopening.
- weighted A*: f = g + w·h, w > 1: trust the heuristic more. Faster, but the path can be up to w times the optimum.

A* is optimal with an admissible h and is as efficient as any algorithm using the same h. Compare the two examples 'Weighted graph for UCS and A*' (admissible h: optimal cost 12, fewer expansions than UCS) and 'Same graph, inadmissible h(B) = 12' (h overestimates, A* returns cost 13 instead of 12). If h is admissible but not monotone, a node may be closed before its cheapest path is known; A* then reopens it when the cheaper path appears: try 'Admissible but not monotone h: A* reopens C'.

Complete: yes. Optimal: yes with admissible h. Time: exponential in general. Space: exponential (OPEN and CLOSED).

- Trap: Admissible ≠ consistent: consistency implies admissibility, not the reverse. Example 'Admissible but not monotone h' has h ≤ h* everywhere yet A* must reopen C.
- Trap: h = 0 makes A* behave like UCS.
- Trap: With an inadmissible h the first goal picked may not be optimal (example 'Same graph, inadmissible h(B) = 12').
- Trap: The goal test is on picking from OPEN, not on generating: the goal can sit on OPEN with a worse g while a cheaper route is still being found.

## Weighted A* (week 5, Graph search · optimal)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-weighted-astar.html

Weighted A* multiplies the heuristic by a factor w ≥ 1. With w = 1 it is A*; with a large w it behaves like Best First Search. You trade optimality for speed, and the trade is controlled: the path is never worse than w times the best one.

Definition: OPEN is ordered on f(N) = g(N) + w·h(N). Everything else is as in A*: a goal test when a node is picked, and cheaper paths update the pair (node, parent, g). If h is admissible (h ≤ h*), the cost of the path returned satisfies cost ≤ w · C*, where C* is the optimal cost. The tracer computes C* with a separate Uniform Cost Search and checks the bound at the end.

Pseudocode:

```
OPEN ← [(S, nil, g=0)] ordered by f = g + w·h
while OPEN not empty
    N ← node with least f;  remove it
    if GoalTest(N): return the path               # cost ≤ w · C*  (admissible h)
    move N to CLOSED
    for each child C with g' = g(N) + k(N,C)
        new: add to OPEN
        cheaper than its pair on OPEN/CLOSED: update parent and g (reopen if CLOSED)
```

- f(N) = g(N) + w·h(N): cost so far plus w times the estimate. w > 1 inflates h, which pulls the search toward the goal.
- cost(path) ≤ w · C*   (h admissible, w ≥ 1): at most w times the optimum. w·h(N) ≤ w·h*(N), so w·h is within a factor w of an admissible estimate, and the first goal picked can be only that much worse than the best.

Fewer expansions than A* on many graphs, at the price of a controlled loss of optimality. It is a good compromise when A* is too slow. The bound is a guarantee, not a prediction: the actual path is often optimal.

Complete: yes. Optimal: no: within w · C* with admissible h. Time: often much less than A*. Space: same as A*.

- Trap: The bound needs an admissible h. With an inadmissible h there is no guarantee at all (try the inadmissible example).
- Trap: w = 1 gives plain A*; w < 1 is not weighted A* (it drifts toward UCS and loses the bound meaning).
- Trap: A larger w does not always expand fewer nodes on every graph; it usually does.
- Trap: The trade in numbers: on the 'Dijkstra demo' graph w = 2 returns S–C–G at cost 9 (optimum 8, bound 2 × 8 = 16) after 3 expansions instead of A*'s 5; on the 4×5 grid w = 2 expands 8 nodes instead of 20 and still finds cost 7. Set w = 1 to get A* back.

## Heuristic comparison (A* with h = 0, h, h*) (week 5, Graph search · optimal)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-heuristic-comparison.html

The quality of a heuristic shows in how much search it saves. Here the same graph is searched by A* with three heuristics: no information (h = 0), the given h, and the perfect h = h*, the true remaining cost.

Definition: A* orders OPEN on f = g + h. With h = 0 it expands nodes in order of g, which is Uniform Cost Search. With h = h* (the exact cost to the goal, computed by Dijkstra from the goal) f is constant along an optimal path, so only that path is expanded (up to ties). An admissible h lies between the two: h ≤ h*, and a larger h (closer to h*) never expands more nodes than a smaller admissible one, apart from ties. **Supplementary:** the effective branching factor b* is not part of the lecture notation; it is the b that makes a uniform tree of depth d (the solution length) hold exactly as many nodes as were generated, 1 + b* + … + b*^d = generated. A smaller b* (closer to 1) means a better heuristic.

Pseudocode:

```
for each heuristic H in [ h = 0,  h (given),  h = h* ]:
    run A* with f = g + H
    record: nodes expanded, nodes generated, path cost
    b* ← the branching factor of a uniform tree of depth d (solution length)
         with the same number of nodes:   generated = 1 + b* + b*² + … + b*^d
compare the three rows
```

- 0 ≤ h ≤ h*  ⇒  expansions(h*) ≤ expansions(h) ≤ expansions(0): a more informed admissible h expands no more nodes (up to ties). A* expands every node with f < C*; raising h raises f and removes nodes from that set.
- generated = 1 + b* + b*² + … + b*^d: effective branching factor (supplementary). It turns a node count into a single branching number that can be compared across problems.

It makes the value of heuristic information concrete. On an inadmissible h the middle row can be cheaper to run but return a worse path: the path cost column then differs from the other two.

Complete: yes. Optimal: yes for h = 0 and h*; yes for h admissible. Time: 3 × A*. Space: 3 × A*.

- Trap: Admissible does not mean good: h = 0 is admissible and almost useless.
- Trap: With an inadmissible h the middle row may have a higher cost than the others (example 'Same graph, inadmissible h(B) = 12': 13 against 12).
- Trap: Ties can make the counts differ by one or two; the ordering of the three rows is what matters.
- Trap: h* needs the true remaining costs, which in practice means already having solved the problem.

## A* on a state space (week 5, Graph search · informed)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/statespace-astar.html

A* adds the cost paid so far to the heuristic estimate of what remains. On the 8-puzzle, with h = tiles out of place or Manhattan distance, it finds a shortest solution while expanding far fewer boards than breadth-first search.

Definition: Node pairs are (state, parent, g) with f = g + h. Every move costs 1, so g is the depth along the current best path. OPEN is ordered by f with alphabetical ties, the goal test is on picking, and a cheaper path to a known state updates its parent. If h never overestimates the true remaining moves (admissible) the first goal picked is optimal.

Pseudocode:

```
OPEN ← [(S, nil, g=0)] ordered by f = g + h
while OPEN not empty
    N ← the pair with the least f;  remove it       # ties: alphabetical
    if GoalTest(N): return the path
    CLOSED ← N : CLOSED
    for each child C of MoveGen(N) with g' = g(N) + 1
        new: add (C, N, g') to OPEN
        cheaper than its pair on OPEN or CLOSED: update parent and g (reopen if CLOSED)
```

- f(N) = g(N) + h(N): paid plus estimated remainder. An estimate of the cheapest solution through N.
- h₁ ≤ h₂ ≤ h*: tiles out of place ≤ Manhattan ≤ true moves left. Each misplaced tile needs ≥ 1 move and each needs ≥ its Manhattan distance, so both are admissible and h₂ dominates h₁: A* with h₂ expands no more states than with h₁.
- missionaries: h = 2·⌈(n − k)/(k − 1)⌉ + 1: n people on the left bank, boat holds k (**supplementary**). Each round trip moves at most k − 1 people across net, and the last trip moves k; ignoring the safety rule only lowers the bound, so it is admissible.

A better (larger, still admissible) h prunes more of the search. Run example space-8-puzzle-12 with each heuristic and compare the 'expanded' count: both return the same 12-move solution, Manhattan after 16 expansions, tiles out of place after 79, and h = 0 does not finish within the 400-expansion cap. (On the easy five-move board space-8-puzzle the two tie at 6.)

Complete: yes. Optimal: yes with admissible h. Time: exponential in general. Space: exponential in general.

- Trap: Admissible is not enough to compare: the larger of two admissible heuristics is better informed.
- Trap: The blank is never counted in either heuristic; counting it can overestimate.
- Trap: With h = 0 (water jugs have no good h) A* degenerates to Uniform Cost Search, here the same as BFS.

## Sequence alignment (dynamic programming) (week 6, Sequence alignment)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/align-dp.html

Comparing two DNA strings means lining them up with as few mismatches and gaps as possible. Every alignment is a path through a grid, so the best alignment is a shortest path, and dynamic programming finds it by filling a table.

Definition: D(i,j) is the cheapest alignment of the first i letters of a with the first j letters of b. Fill the table from D(0,0) = 0 using three moves: diagonal (pair two letters), down (a letter of a against a gap), right (a letter of b against a gap). Trace back from D(m,n).

Pseudocode:

```
D(0,0) ← 0;  D(i,0) ← i·gap;  D(0,j) ← j·gap
for i ← 1..m, for j ← 1..n
    D(i,j) ← min( D(i−1,j−1) + cost(aᵢ, bⱼ),     # diagonal: match or mismatch
                  D(i−1,j)   + gap,               # down: aᵢ against a gap
                  D(i,j−1)   + gap )              # right: bⱼ against a gap
trace back from (m,n) choosing a move that produced each value
```

- D(i,j) = min{ D(i−1,j−1) + c(aᵢ,bⱼ), D(i−1,j) + gap, D(i,j−1) + gap }: best of: pair the letters, gap in b, gap in a. Every alignment of the prefixes ends in exactly one of these three ways, so the minimum over them is optimal (optimal substructure).

Exact and O(m·n). The same lattice can be searched by A* with an admissible heuristic, or with frontier ideas to cut memory, which is how the course connects alignment to search.

Complete: yes. Optimal: yes. Time: O(m·n). Space: O(m·n).

- Trap: Costs are minimised here; scoring versions maximise similarity instead.
- Trap: Off-by-one: row i refers to letter aᵢ, i.e. a[i−1] in code.
- Trap: Several alignments can share the optimal cost; the traceback prefers the diagonal move on ties, so a different tie-break prints a different but equally good alignment.
- Trap: The costs decide the shape: in 'ACGTC vs AGTC, gap 2, mismatch 3' the single gap that the length difference forces goes after the A, where it lets G, T and C match exactly (cost 2); anywhere else it would add mismatches of 3 each.

## A* with upper-bound pruning of OPEN (week 6, Graph search · space saving)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-astar-ub.html

OPEN is where A* spends much of its memory. If we already know some solution of cost U, any node whose estimate f = g + h exceeds U cannot be on a cheaper solution (with an admissible h), so it is not worth storing. **Supplementary:** this is the bound used in Zhou and Hansen's space-saving A* variants; it is not in the lecture slides.

Definition: Run A* as usual, but when a child C is generated with f(C) = g(C) + h(C) > U, drop it instead of adding it to OPEN. U can be given or obtained cheaply, for instance from greedy best-first search. If OPEN becomes empty without reaching the goal, the quick solution that produced U is returned.

Pseudocode:

```
U ← cost of a quick solution (greedy by h) or a given bound
OPEN ← [(S, nil, 0)]
while OPEN not empty
    N ← node with least f = g + h;  remove it
    if GoalTest(N): return the path
    move N to CLOSED
    for each child C with g' = g(N) + k(N,C)
        if g' + h(C) > U: discard C  (never enters OPEN)
        else add / update C exactly as A* does
return the quick solution if OPEN empties (it was optimal or h was inadmissible)
```

- discard C when g(C) + h(C) > U: the best possible cost through C is already worse than a known solution. With h ≤ h*, g(C) + h(C) never overestimates the cheapest solution through C, so such a C cannot improve on U.
- C* ≤ U: the optimum is at most the bound. U is the cost of a real solution. A bound below C* would wrongly discard every solution; the run then reports failure.

A better bound prunes more: on the 'Dijkstra demo' graph the greedy bound U = 9 keeps peak OPEN at 2 where A* needs 3. The saving is on OPEN only: CLOSED is as large as in A*. Combine with CLOSED-pruning methods (BFHS, SMGS) for real savings.

Complete: yes if U ≥ C*. Optimal: yes with admissible h and U ≥ C*. Time: at most A*'s. Space: OPEN smaller than A*, CLOSED same.

- Trap: With an inadmissible h, a node with f > U may still lead to a cheaper path, so pruning can lose the optimum (the search then falls back to the quick solution).
- Trap: A bound that is too small yields no solution at all.
- Trap: Nodes with f = U are kept: they may still give a solution of cost exactly U.

## Sequence alignment (A*) (week 6, Sequence alignment)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/align-astar.html

Dynamic programming fills the whole table. A* treats alignment as a shortest-path search on the same lattice and, with a good heuristic, explores only the part of the table near the best alignment.

Definition: States are lattice points (i,j); moves are diagonal, down and right with their costs. h(i,j) = gap × |(m−i) − (n−j)| because the remaining length difference must be covered by gaps.

Pseudocode:

```
start (0,0), goal (m,n)
moves: diagonal cost(aᵢ,bⱼ), down gap, right gap
h(i,j) = gap · |(m − i) − (n − j)|           # admissible: the length difference must be covered by gaps
run A*: pick least f = g + h from OPEN; update cheaper paths; stop when (m,n) is picked
```

- h(i,j) = gap · |(m − i) − (n − j)|: at least this many gaps are unavoidable. Each gap shortens the length difference by one, so this many gap moves remain in any completion: h never overestimates.

Optimal like dynamic programming, usually with fewer states: the more alike the sequences, the fewer lattice points A* has to expand, because the cheap diagonal path keeps f low and everything else waits on OPEN. With large sequences, frontier search and DCFS keep its memory small.

Complete: yes. Optimal: yes. Time: ≤ O(m·n·log(m·n)). Space: ≤ O(m·n).

- Trap: A weak h (such as 0) makes A* behave like Dijkstra and expand most of the table. When both sequences have the same length h is 0 at the start, so the saving comes only from the cheap diagonal moves: compare 'ACGTTGCAAT vs ACGTAGCAAT, one substitution' (11 of 121 points) with 'ACGTAC vs TGCATG, unrelated' (19 of 49).
- Trap: A* is only guaranteed to find the optimal cost, not a unique alignment: several alignments can tie, and the tie-break decides which one is shown.

## Breadth First Heuristic Search (BFHS) (week 6, Graph search · space saving)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-bfhs.html

A* remembers every node it has expanded. Breadth First Heuristic Search borrows breadth-first search's layering: it knows that a node can only be regenerated from a neighbouring layer, so older layers can be thrown away. An upper bound U on f keeps the layers narrow. **Supplementary:** BFHS is from Zhou and Hansen's work on memory-bounded graph search; it is beyond the lecture slides.

Definition: Layer k holds the nodes reached with k moves. Expand layer k completely to build layer k+1. A child is discarded if f = g + h > U. Duplicate detection looks only at the current layer, the previous layer and the layer being built, which is enough on undirected graphs and means all earlier layers can be deleted. When a goal is picked with g < U, U shrinks to g. The search ends when a layer is empty.

Pseudocode:

```
U ← cost of a quick solution (greedy) or a given bound
layer0 ← [S]
while the current layer is not empty
    for each node N in the layer (least f first)
        if GoalTest(N) and g(N) < U: remember N, U ← g(N)
        else for each child C:  if g(C) + h(C) > U: discard
                                 elif C is already in the current, previous or next layer with g ≤ g(C): skip
                                 else put C in the next layer
    delete the layer before the previous one          # keep only the boundary
    move to the next layer
return the best goal found (or the quick solution)
```

- CLOSED = layers k and k−1: only the boundary is stored. Every neighbour of a layer-k node is in layer k−1, k or k+1 (in a graph of unit moves), so older layers can never be regenerated through duplicate detection.
- discard C when g(C) + h(C) > U: bound pruning. It keeps the layers narrow and, with h ≤ h*, never discards the optimal path when U ≥ C*.

BFHS stores far fewer expanded nodes than A* on graphs whose layers are narrow compared with the whole explored region: on the 4×5 grid its peak CLOSED is 8 against A*'s 19. It pays with expanding every node with f ≤ U, even ones A* would never reach.

Complete: yes if U ≥ C*. Optimal: yes with admissible h. Time: A*-like. Space: two layers + one.

- Trap: Costs are compared across layers, so a node can be reached in a later layer with a lower g; this tracer keeps the cheaper copy only when it is still in a retained layer.
- Trap: A bad (large) U weakens the pruning but never breaks the answer.
- Trap: In the original BFHS no parent pointers are kept, so only the cost is known; here parent links are kept just to print the path. Divide and Conquer BFHS shows how to recover it without them.

## Divide and Conquer BFHS (DC-BFHS) (week 6, Graph search · space saving)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-dc-bfhs.html

Deleting layers saves memory but loses the parent pointers needed to print the path. Divide and Conquer BFHS keeps one thing instead: the middle node of the best path. Each half is then a smaller search of the same kind. **Supplementary:** from Zhou and Hansen; the relay idea matches Divide and Conquer Frontier Search from the course. The beam-search version (DC beam search) is not implemented here.

Definition: Run BFHS to find the optimal cost C and the layer count L. Run it again with every node on layer ⌊L/2⌋ acting as a relay: its descendants carry the relay's name and its g. The goal's relay R splits the problem into S→R (cost g(R)) and R→T (cost C − g(R)). Solve each recursively; in the sub-searches the exact cost is the upper bound U and h = 0 (the original h aims at T, not R).

Pseudocode:

```
DC-BFHS(S, T, U):
    run BFHS from S to T with bound U, no parent pointers      # gives cost C and the number of layers L
    if L ≤ 1: return [S, T]
    run it again, each node at layer ⌊L/2⌋ becoming its own relay and passing it on to descendants
    R ← the relay of the best goal, with g(R)
    return DC-BFHS(S, R, g(R)) ++ DC-BFHS(R, T, C − g(R))      # drop the repeated R
```

- C = g(R) + cost(R→T): an optimal path through R splits into two optimal halves. Each half of an optimal path is itself optimal, so solving the halves and joining them gives an optimal whole.
- memory ≈ boundary layers of the largest sub-search: no pointers, no deep layers. The sub-searches run one at a time, so their memory is not added up.

Shows how to get the path from a search that keeps almost nothing: on the 4×5 grid the boundary CLOSED is at most 9 against A*'s 19. The cost is a second pass per level of recursion.

Complete: yes if U ≥ C*. Optimal: yes with admissible h. Time: ≈ 2 × BFHS. Space: boundary layers.

- Trap: The relay must be recorded in the same run that finds the best goal; a different tie-break could give a different path and relay.
- Trap: A sub-search uses h = 0, so it expands more nodes than the first run did.
- Trap: The relay layer ⌊L/2⌋ is by number of moves, not by cost; on weighted graphs the halves can have unequal cost.

## Beam Stack Search (week 6, Graph search · space saving)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-beam-stack.html

Plain beam search forgets nodes outside the beam and can miss the goal. Beam stack search keeps a small record of what was forgotten: for every layer, the interval of f values it has already covered. When the search runs dry it backtracks and goes after the part of f-space it skipped. **Supplementary:** this is Zhou and Hansen's algorithm; it is not in the lecture slides.

Definition: Layer k holds nodes reached with k moves, at most w of them. The beam stack has one item [lo, hi) per layer. Children of layer k go to layer k+1 only if f is in [lo, hi) and f ≤ U. If there are more than w, the w with least f survive and hi becomes the f of the best node dropped. When a layer has no children (dead end or goal), backtrack to the deepest layer with hi < U, set lo ← hi and hi ← ∞, and rebuild that layer from the one above. Ties in f are broken alphabetically, so the intervals are over (f, name) pairs and the search always terminates.

Pseudocode:

```
U ← cost of a quick solution (greedy) or a given bound
layer 0 ← [S];  beam stack ← [ [lo=−∞, hi=∞) per layer ]
loop
    if a node of the current layer is the goal and g < U: remember it, U ← g
    candidates ← children of the layer with f ≤ U and f in [lo, hi) of the next layer's stack item
    if more than w candidates: keep the w with least f, set hi of that item to the f of the best discarded one
    if the next layer is non-empty: go down one layer
    else BACKTRACK: pop to the deepest layer whose hi < U;  lo ← hi, hi ← ∞;  rebuild that layer
    stop when no layer has hi left to explore
return the best goal found
```

- stored nodes ≤ w · (layers): each layer holds at most w nodes. The beam width bounds the memory regardless of the graph.
- layer k item = [lo_k, hi_k): f-values already covered up to hi_k. Every dropped node has f ≥ hi_k, so once all slices are searched nothing with f ≤ U is missed; with admissible h the optimum is found.

On the 4×5 grid with w = 2 it stores at most 14 nodes where A* stores 20, at the price of 40 expansions against A*'s 19 (it backtracks 3 times). A wide enough beam makes it behave like A*; w = 1 turns it into depth-first-like backtracking. Memory stays small either way, so it trades time for space.

Complete: yes (with backtracking). Optimal: yes with admissible h. Time: up to exponential. Space: O(w · depth).

- Trap: With w = 1 it can revisit the same node many times.
- Trap: A bound U that is too low prunes the solution; the greedy bound is always safe.
- Trap: The cost equals UCS/A* only when h is admissible; with an inadmissible h it returns the best path it saw, which may not be optimal.
- Trap: Cycles are avoided here by never generating a node that is already on its own path.

## Smart Memory Graph Search (SMGS) (week 6, Graph search · space saving)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-smgs.html

A* keeps every expanded node in CLOSED for two reasons: to avoid regenerating it, and to read the path back. A node whose neighbours have all been expanded can no longer be regenerated, so the first reason is gone. The second still holds for nodes on the way to the frontier. SMGS deletes the rest. The name and the idea of a boundary and relay nodes follow the lecture material on space-saving search; the exact deletion rule below is this site's reading of it, so treat the details as **supplementary**.

Definition: Run A*. After each expansion classify every CLOSED node. Boundary: at least one neighbour has not been expanded yet, so it may still be regenerated. Interior: all neighbours are expanded. A relay node is an interior node that is an ancestor, through parent pointers, of an OPEN or boundary node. Delete interior nodes that are not relays. The path to the goal is read from the nodes that remain.

Pseudocode:

```
OPEN ← [(S, nil, 0)];  CLOSED ← empty
while OPEN not empty
    N ← node with least f;  remove it
    if GoalTest(N): return the path (follow parents through the kept nodes)
    move N to CLOSED;  generate children as in A*
    for each X in CLOSED:
        if every neighbour of X has been expanded:  X is interior
    live ← OPEN ∪ {CLOSED nodes that are not interior}      # the boundary
    relay ← interior nodes that are ancestors of a live node
    delete every interior node that is not a relay
```

- |CLOSED| ≤ |boundary| + |relay|: only the edge of the expanded region plus the needed ancestors. Everything else is deleted, so on wide graphs CLOSED is a thin shell instead of a solid blob.

Saves CLOSED memory at no cost in nodes expanded (on the 4×5 grid it deletes 9 nodes and the peak CLOSED falls from 19 to 17; the saving grows with the size of the graph). The relay rule is conservative: it keeps whole parent chains. Divide and conquer methods (DCFS, DC-BFHS) cut even those.

Complete: yes. Optimal: yes with admissible h. Time: same as A*. Space: boundary + relay nodes.

- Trap: If an h is inconsistent a node can be reopened with a better g; its deleted neighbours are simply regenerated as new nodes.
- Trap: Savings depend on the graph: on a tree or a path nearly every node stays a boundary or relay node.

## Admissibility & monotone check (week 6, Graph search · optimal)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-monotone-check.html

A* is only as good as its heuristic. Two properties matter: admissibility (never overestimate the remaining cost) and the monotone or consistency condition (the estimate never drops by more than the cost of an edge). This tool checks both on any graph.

Definition: Compute the true remaining cost h*(n) to the goal by Dijkstra's algorithm from the goal. h is admissible if h(n) ≤ h*(n) everywhere. h is monotone if h(m) ≤ k(m,n) + h(n) for every edge (m,n).

Pseudocode:

```
h* ← Dijkstra from the goal (true cost to the goal)
for each node n: admissible at n  ⇔  h(n) ≤ h*(n)
for each edge (m, n) with cost k: monotone  ⇔  h(m) ≤ k + h(n)   (both directions if undirected)
monotone everywhere and h(goal) = 0  ⇒  admissible
```

- admissible: h(n) ≤ h*(n): never overestimate. A* then never discards the optimal path.
- monotone: h(m) − h(n) ≤ k(m,n): the estimate drops by at most the edge cost. Then f(n) = g(n) + h(n) ≥ g(m) + h(m) = f(m): f never decreases, so a node is closed with its optimal g and never reopened.
- monotone ∧ h(goal) = 0 ⇒ admissible: consistency is the stronger property. Summing the edge inequalities along the optimal path gives h(n) ≤ h*(n).

Knowing which property holds tells you whether A* is optimal (admissible) and whether it may need to reopen closed nodes (not monotone).

Complete: n/a. Optimal: n/a. Time: O(E log V). Space: O(V).

- Trap: Admissible does not imply monotone: the 'Admissible but not monotone h' example passes the first table and fails on the edge B→C (3 > 1 + 0); A* then reopens C.
- Trap: Check both directions of an undirected edge.

## Frontier Search (week 6, Graph search · space saving)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-frontier.html

In A* the CLOSED list does two jobs: it stops the search regenerating nodes it has already expanded, and it lets us rebuild the path. Frontier search replaces the first job with a few bits on each OPEN node, and drops CLOSED entirely. This is in the course's discussion of memory-saving search (frontier search and its divide and conquer version); the used-operator bits are shown here in their simplest form, so treat the exact bookkeeping as **supplementary**.

Definition: Each OPEN node stores the set of neighbours that have already been expanded and generated it (its used operators). When N is expanded it never generates a child in used(N). Children already on OPEN merge: the new parent is added to their used set and the cheaper g is kept. After expansion N is discarded. Because no expanded node is stored, the search returns the cost; the path needs a relay recursion (see Divide and Conquer Frontier Search).

Pseudocode:

```
OPEN ← [(S, g=0, used={})]                 # no CLOSED list
while OPEN not empty
    N ← node with least f;  remove it
    if GoalTest(N): return its cost
    for each child C of N with g' = g(N) + k(N,C), if C is not in used(N):
        if C is on OPEN: used(C) ← used(C) ∪ {N};  if g' is lower, update g(C)
        else add (C, g', used = {N}) to OPEN
    (N itself is forgotten)
```

- memory = |OPEN|: there is no CLOSED list. In grid-like graphs the frontier is a thin front, much smaller than everything expanded so far.
- h consistent (h(N) ≤ k(N,M) + h(M)): needed for correctness. Then a node is expanded with its final g, so never needing to be reopened. Reversible moves (undirected graph) are also needed, so the used bit can be set.

A* minus its biggest list: on the 4×5 grid it holds at most 5 nodes in total where A* holds 20 (19 of them CLOSED). It trades away the path: on its own it can only report the cost, and DCFS or DC-BFHS recover the path.

Complete: yes. Optimal: yes with admissible, consistent h. Time: same as A*. Space: OPEN only.

- Trap: With an inconsistent heuristic a node may need reopening, which frontier search cannot do: on 'Admissible but not monotone h: A* reopens C' it returns S–C–G = 6 although the optimum is 5 (A* reopens C and finds S–A–B–C–G).
- Trap: Only for undirected graphs here: a directed edge has no 'reverse operator' to mark as used.
- Trap: To print the path this tracer carries the path along with each OPEN node. That is for the display only and is not counted in the memory figures.

## IDA* (week 6, Graph search · space saving)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-ida-star.html

A* is optimal but can run out of memory because OPEN grows exponentially. IDA* gets the same answer using memory proportional to the path length, by running depth-first searches with a growing cost limit.

Definition: Repeat depth-first search from the start, refusing to go past any node whose f = g + h exceeds the current bound. The first bound is h(start); each next bound is the smallest f that was cut off in the previous pass.

Pseudocode:

```
bound ← f(S) = h(S)
loop
    t ← DFS(S, g = 0, bound)          # depth-first, nodes on the current path are not revisited
    if t = FOUND: return the path
    if t = ∞: return failure
    bound ← t                          # smallest f that exceeded the bound

DFS(N, g, bound):
    f ← g + h(N);  if f > bound: return f
    if GoalTest(N): return FOUND
    min ← ∞
    for each child C not on the path: t ← DFS(C, g + k(N,C), bound); if FOUND: return FOUND; min ← min(min, t)
    return min
```

- bound₀ = h(S),  boundₖ₊₁ = min { f(N) : f(N) > boundₖ }: raise the limit just enough to let in the next cheapest nodes. Never skipping a cost level means the first solution found is the cheapest.
- f(N) = g(N) + h(N): cost so far plus estimated remainder. Same evaluation as A*.

Optimal with admissible h and linear memory. It repeats work in every pass, which is cheap when f takes few distinct values and expensive when many nodes have different f.

Complete: yes. Optimal: yes with admissible h. Time: A* × number of bounds (worst case). Space: O(b·d).

- Trap: Count expansions across all passes: on 'RBFS switches branches...' the bounds are 5, 6, 7 and the passes expand S, A (bound 5); S, A, B (bound 6); S, A, C (bound 7) and reach G: 8 expansions in total against A*'s 4 (the price of linear memory); the table lists every bound.
- Trap: The next bound is the smallest f that was cut off, not bound + 1: costs of 1.5 or 2 would skip values if it were incremented.
- Trap: IDA* has no CLOSED list, so on graphs it may revisit nodes by different paths.

## Recursive Best-First Search (week 6, Graph search · space saving)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-rbfs.html

Recursive Best-First Search behaves like A* but stores only the current path. When the path it is exploring becomes worse than the best alternative elsewhere, it remembers how good that path turned out to be and switches.

Definition: At each node, expand the child with the lowest backed-up value F while it stays below a limit (the best alternative higher up). When it exceeds the limit, return and replace the child's F by the best value found below it.

Pseudocode:

```
RBFS(N, fm(N), limit):
    if GoalTest(N): return SUCCESS
    children ← MoveGen(N) not on the current path
    for each child C: fm(C) ← max(g(C) + h(C), fm(N))     # inherit a backed-up value
    loop
        best ← child with least F;  if fm(best) > limit: return FAIL, fm(best)
        alt ← second least F (∞ if none)
        result, fm(best) ← RBFS(best, fm(best), min(limit, alt))
        if result = SUCCESS: return SUCCESS
call RBFS(S, h(S), ∞)
```

- F(C) = max( g(C) + h(C), F(N) )  for a child C of N: a child inherits its parent's backed-up value when that is larger. When a subtree is abandoned, its F is replaced by the best (smallest) F that was cut off below it. RBFS can then return to a forgotten subtree knowing exactly how promising it was, and the max keeps F from falling below what is already known.

Linear space and optimal with admissible h. It may re-expand the same nodes many times when the best path keeps switching.

Complete: yes. Optimal: yes with admissible h. Time: can exceed A*. Space: O(b·d).

- Trap: The limit passed down is the second-best F, not the parent's f.
- Trap: Keep backed-up values; recomputing g + h throws the information away.
- Trap: RBFS forgets subtrees, so it re-expands them: on 'RBFS switches branches...' A is expanded twice (A* expands each node once), and on ties it can switch back and forth often.

## Divide & Conquer Frontier Search (week 6, Graph search · space saving)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-dcfs.html

Most of A*'s memory is the CLOSED list, kept only to avoid regenerating expanded nodes and to rebuild the path. Frontier search drops CLOSED altogether; Divide and Conquer Frontier Search then rebuilds the path from a node remembered halfway along it.

Definition: Run best-first search keeping only OPEN. Each OPEN node records which neighbours already used an edge into it, so expanded nodes are never regenerated. Each node also carries a relay node from the middle of its path. Once the goal is reached, solve start→relay and relay→goal the same way, recursively.

Pseudocode:

```
DCFS(S, G):
    run frontier search from S to G           # OPEN only; each node keeps a 'used' set of neighbours
        each node carries relay = the first node on its path with g ≥ C/2   (C = estimate f(S))
    if G is next to S: return [S, G]
    R ← relay of G
    return DCFS(S, R) ++ DCFS(R, G)       # (dropping the repeated R)
```

- memory ≈ |frontier|, not |frontier| + |expanded|: only the boundary of the search is stored. For grid-like spaces (such as sequence alignment) the frontier is much smaller than the expanded region.

On the 4×5 grid the frontier never holds more than a handful of nodes and no CLOSED list is stored, at the cost of 66 expansions in total against A*'s 20. Trades extra time (the recursive searches) for a large memory saving. It is the basis of memory-efficient sequence alignment.

Complete: yes. Optimal: yes with admissible h. Time: a small multiple of one search. Space: frontier only.

- Trap: Frontier search alone gives the cost, not the path: the relay recursion recovers it.
- Trap: The 'used' bookkeeping is what replaces the CLOSED check.

## Minimax (week 7, Game playing)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/game-minimax.html

In a two-player game one player (MAX) wants a high score and the other (MIN) a low one. Minimax looks ahead to the end of the tree and assumes both play perfectly: MAX picks the child with the largest value, MIN the smallest.

Definition: Evaluate leaves with the evaluation function e. Back values up the tree: a MAX node's value is the maximum of its children, a MIN node's value is the minimum. The root's value is the guaranteed outcome.

Pseudocode:

```
Minimax(N):
    if N is a leaf: return e(N)
    if N is MAX: return max over children C of Minimax(C)
    if N is MIN: return min over children C of Minimax(C)
```

- v(N) = max over C of v(C) at MAX,  min over C of v(C) at MIN: back up the best reply at every level. Assuming the opponent replies optimally, this is the best value MAX can guarantee.

Correct but exhaustive: it evaluates every leaf, b^d of them.

Complete: yes (finite tree). Optimal: yes against an optimal opponent. Time: O(b^d). Space: O(b·d).

- Trap: Values are always from MAX's point of view.
- Trap: Evaluate left to right; the order matters for alpha-beta, not for minimax.

## Alpha-Beta pruning (week 7, Game playing)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/game-alpha-beta.html

Alpha-beta gives the same answer as minimax while skipping parts of the tree that cannot change the decision. If you already know a move gives you 3, you can stop examining another move as soon as you see the opponent can hold you to 2 there.

Definition: Pass a window (α, β) down the tree. α is the best value MAX is already guaranteed, β the best value MIN is guaranteed. At a MAX node raise α; at a MIN node lower β; as soon as α ≥ β, prune the remaining children.

Pseudocode:

```
AlphaBeta(N, α, β):
    if N is a leaf: return e(N)
    if N is MAX:
        for each child C: α ← max(α, AlphaBeta(C, α, β)); if α ≥ β: prune the rest (β cut-off)
        return α
    if N is MIN:
        for each child C: β ← min(β, AlphaBeta(C, α, β)); if α ≥ β: prune the rest (α cut-off)
        return β
call AlphaBeta(root, −∞, +∞)
```

- prune when α ≥ β: the window is empty. MIN above will never allow a value ≥ β, and MAX above already has α: nothing in this subtree can affect the root.
- best case ≈ b^(d/2) leaves: with perfect move ordering. Good ordering lets each MIN node be refuted by its first child, effectively doubling the search depth for the same work.

Always returns the minimax value. How much it prunes depends on move ordering: try the 'best first' and 'worst first' settings.

Complete: yes. Optimal: same value as minimax. Time: O(b^(d/2)) best, O(b^d) worst. Space: O(b·d).

- Trap: Pruned subtrees are never evaluated: count leaves carefully.
- Trap: How much is pruned depends on the move ordering, never the value: on example game-four-ply the Child order parameter gives 10 leaves (as given), 7 (best first) and 15 (worst first), all with value 8.
- Trap: The value returned at a pruned node is a bound, not an exact value; only the root's value is exact.

## SSS* (week 7, Game playing)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/game-sss-star.html

SSS* treats game-tree search as best-first search over strategies. It keeps an OPEN list of node triples and always refines the most promising one, so it never looks at a leaf that alpha-beta would skip, and sometimes skips leaves alpha-beta looks at.

Definition: OPEN holds triples (node, status, merit) where status is LIVE (not yet examined) or SOLVED. Starting from (root, LIVE, +∞), repeatedly take the triple with the highest merit and apply one of the six cases until the root is SOLVED; its merit is the minimax value.

Pseudocode:

```
OPEN ← [(root, LIVE, +∞)]
loop
    (J, s, h) ← triple with the highest merit (ties: leftmost)
    if J = root and s = SOLVED: return h
    if s = LIVE:
        leaf      → insert (J, SOLVED, min(h, e(J)))
        MAX node  → insert (C, LIVE, h) for every child C
        MIN node  → insert (first child, LIVE, h)
    if s = SOLVED:
        J's parent is MAX → insert (parent, SOLVED, h); purge every other descendant of the parent
        J's parent is MIN → next sibling exists: insert (sibling, LIVE, h)
                            else insert (parent, SOLVED, h)
```

- merit h = upper bound on the value of the best strategy through the node: how good this line could still be for MAX. Taking the highest merit first is best-first search; the first solved root has the true value.

Dominates alpha-beta in leaves evaluated, at the cost of an OPEN list that can grow large.

Complete: yes. Optimal: minimax value. Time: ≤ alpha-beta leaves. Space: O(b^(d/2)).

- Trap: Ties in merit are broken by leftmost position.
- Trap: SSS* never evaluates more leaves than alpha-beta with the same left-to-right order (game-four-ply: 8 against 10) but keeps a large OPEN list.
- Trap: When a MAX parent is solved, remove all its other descendants from OPEN.

## Expectiminimax (supplementary) (week 7, Game playing)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/game-expectiminimax.html

**Supplementary (Russell & Norvig): not in the course lectures.** In backgammon-like games a die roll lies between your move and the opponent's reply. Expectiminimax adds a third kind of node, the chance node, whose value is the average of its outcomes weighted by their probabilities.

Definition: Leaves hold e(N) for MAX. A MAX node backs up the maximum of its children, a MIN node the minimum, and a chance node the expected value Σ P(C)·v(C), where the probabilities on its outgoing edges sum to 1. The chance nodes do not change whose turn it is: in this studio a chance node sits between a player's move and the next player's node.

Pseudocode:

```
Expectiminimax(N):
    if N is a leaf: return e(N)
    if N is MAX:    return max over children C of Expectiminimax(C)
    if N is MIN:    return min over children C of Expectiminimax(C)
    if N is CHANCE: return Σ over children C of P(C) · Expectiminimax(C)
```

- v(chance) = Σ over outcomes C of P(C) · v(C): the expected value of the roll. Neither player controls the dice, so the best estimate of a position before the roll is its average over the outcomes.

Showing that values matter, not just their order: with chance nodes only the numbers (not merely which leaf is bigger) decide the move, so the evaluation function must be a proper scale. Alpha-beta and SSS* in this studio decline trees with chance nodes because their pruning rules assume pure MAX/MIN.

Complete: yes (finite tree). Optimal: maximises expected value against an optimal opponent. Time: O(b^d · n^d). Space: O(b·d).

- Trap: A chance node's value can be a fraction that is not any leaf's value.
- Trap: Probabilities on the edges of one chance node must sum to 1.
- Trap: Treating chance nodes as MIN, MAX or a plain average gives a wrong value or a wrong move: the last caption on example game-chance-gamble lists them (4, 8 and 5 against the true 6.5).
- Trap: Minimax would be wrong here: it treats the roll as a choice. Pruning is also harder, because an average is only bounded if the leaf values are.

## Forward state-space planning (week 8, Planning)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/plan-forward.html

A planning problem gives an initial state, a goal and operators described in STRIPS form: each operator has preconditions, an add list and a delete list. In the blocks world the operators are pickup, putdown, stack and unstack, and AE means the arm is empty. Forward planning simply searches the state space from the initial state.

Definition: Breadth-first search where a node is a state (a set of facts) and an edge applies an operator whose preconditions hold: S' = (S − delete) ∪ add.

Pseudocode:

```
OPEN ← [(init, plan = [ ])];  seen ← {init}
while OPEN not empty
    (S, plan) ← head(OPEN)
    if goal ⊆ S: return plan
    for each operator O with pre(O) ⊆ S
        S' ← (S − del(O)) ∪ add(O)
        if S' not seen: append (S', plan + [O])
return failure
```

- S' = (S − del(O)) ∪ add(O): remove the delete list, add the add list. The STRIPS assumption: an action changes only what it explicitly says.

Simple and complete, but the branching factor is every applicable action, most of them irrelevant to the goal.

Complete: yes. Optimal: shortest plan (BFS). Time: O(b^d). Space: O(b^d).

- Trap: Applicable is not the same as relevant: forward search wastes effort on irrelevant actions.

## Backward state-space planning (week 8, Planning)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/plan-backward.html

A planning problem gives an initial state, a goal and operators described in STRIPS form: each operator has preconditions, an add list and a delete list. In the blocks world the operators are pickup, putdown, stack and unstack, and AE means the arm is empty. Backward planning starts from the goal and asks which action could have achieved it last.

Definition: Search over goal sets. An operator is relevant if it adds at least one goal and deletes none. Regressing goal set G through it gives (G − add) ∪ pre. Stop when the initial state satisfies the goal set.

Pseudocode:

```
OPEN ← [(goal, plan = [ ])]
while OPEN not empty
    (G, plan) ← head(OPEN)
    if G ⊆ init: return plan
    for each operator O that adds some g ∈ G and deletes nothing in G
        G' ← (G − add(O)) ∪ pre(O)
        if G' is consistent and new: append (G', [O] + plan)
```

- regress(G, O) = (G − add(O)) ∪ pre(O): goals the action achieves are dropped, its preconditions are added. These are exactly the facts needed before O so that G holds after O.

Focused on the goal, so the branching factor is small, but goal sets can be impossible (like holding a block with the arm empty) and must be pruned.

Complete: yes. Optimal: shortest plan (BFS). Time: O(b^d) with smaller b. Space: O(b^d).

- Trap: Discard inconsistent goal sets.
- Trap: An operator that deletes a goal cannot be the last step.

## Goal Stack Planning (week 8, Planning)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/plan-gsp.html

A planning problem gives an initial state, a goal and operators described in STRIPS form: each operator has preconditions, an add list and a delete list. In the blocks world the operators are pickup, putdown, stack and unstack, and AE means the arm is empty. Goal Stack Planning, the strategy of STRIPS, works through the goals one at a time using a stack.

Definition: Push the conjunctive goal and its parts. Pop goals that hold. Replace an unsatisfied goal with an operator that achieves it and that operator's preconditions. When an operator reaches the top, apply it and add it to the plan. Re-check conjunctions, because later actions can undo earlier goals.

Pseudocode:

```
push the conjunct goal, then each goal in it
while the stack is not empty
    x ← top
    if x is a goal that holds in the state: pop
    elif x is an unsatisfied goal: push an action O that achieves it, then O's preconditions (conjunct and each)
    elif x is a conjunct: if all hold pop, else push its unsatisfied goals again
    elif x is an action: pop, apply it to the state, append it to the plan
```

- linear planning: solve g₁, then g₂, … in order: one goal at a time. Fine for independent goals; interacting goals (Sussman anomaly) make it undo its own work.

Fast and easy to trace, but not optimal and sensitive to goal order: on the Sussman anomaly it needs 10 steps where 6 suffice.

Complete: no. Optimal: no. Time: linear in plan length (when it works). Space: O(plan length).

- Trap: Push preconditions so that the one to achieve first is on top.
- Trap: Always re-check the conjunct goal after its parts are popped.
- Trap: Goal clobbering: achieving one goal can undo another (the Sussman anomaly). Run example plan-sussman: 10 steps instead of 6; the captions say 'Goal clobbering' when it happens.

## Graphplan (week 8, Planning)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/plan-graphplan.html

Graphplan builds a layered graph in polynomial time that over-approximates what can be true after each number of steps, then does a much smaller backward search inside it. The graph alternates proposition layers P0, P1, … and action layers A0, A1, …. A no-op (persistence) action carries each proposition unchanged to the next layer. Mutex pairs record things that can never hold together (propositions) or be done together (actions) at that level.

Definition: Layer P0 is the initial state. Action layer Ai holds every action whose preconditions are all in Pi and pairwise non-mutex, plus a no-op for each proposition. Pi+1 holds every add effect. Two actions in the same layer are mutex by: (1) inconsistent effects, one adds what the other deletes; (2) interference, one deletes a precondition of the other; (3) competing needs, a precondition of one is mutex with a precondition of the other in Pi. Two propositions in Pi+1 are mutex by inconsistent support: every pair of actions that achieve them is mutex. When all goals are in a layer and pairwise non-mutex, extract a plan backwards: choose a set of non-mutex actions achieving the goals, make their preconditions the subgoals one layer earlier, and repeat; a goal set that fails at a layer is remembered as a nogood. Actions in one layer are mutually non-mutex so they may be done in any order, which gives the flat plan.

Pseudocode:

```
P0 ← initial state;  i ← 0
loop
    if all goals ∈ Pi and no two goals are mutex in Pi:
        plan ← EXTRACT(goals, i);  if plan ≠ failure: return plan
    if graph has levelled off and nogoods stopped growing: return failure
    Ai ← actions whose preconditions are in Pi and pairwise non-mutex, plus a no-op for every proposition
    mark action mutexes: inconsistent effects, interference, competing needs
    Pi+1 ← all add-effects of Ai
    mark proposition mutexes: inconsistent support (every pair of achievers is mutex)
    i ← i + 1

EXTRACT(G, i):  if i = 0 return [ ]
    if G ∈ nogood(i) return failure
    choose non-mutex actions in Ai−1 that achieve every g ∈ G (try no-ops first)
    G' ← union of their preconditions;  plan ← EXTRACT(G', i−1)
    if none works: add G to nogood(i); return failure
```

- p, q mutex in Pi+1  ⇔  every achiever of p is mutex with every achiever of q: inconsistent support. If no non-mutex pair of actions can make both, they cannot both be true after that step.
- a, b mutex  ⇐  add(a) ∩ del(b) ≠ ∅  or  del(a) ∩ pre(b) ≠ ∅  or  pre(a) and pre(b) contain a mutex pair: inconsistent effects, interference, competing needs. Each rule names a way the two actions cannot both be carried out in one parallel step.

Mutex reasoning prunes huge numbers of impossible combinations cheaply before any search, and the first layer in which the goals are non-mutex is a lower bound on the plan length (the plan returned has the fewest layers).

Complete: yes (finds a plan whenever one exists). Optimal: fewest layers. Time: graph: polynomial; extraction: exponential in the worst case. Space: polynomial in propositions × layers.

- Trap: Goals appearing without mutex is necessary, not sufficient: extraction can still fail and the graph must be extended.
- Trap: A no-op is an action: it can be mutex with real actions (for example a no-op that keeps AE true is mutex with any action that deletes AE).
- Trap: Layers count parallel steps; in the one-arm blocks world nearly every pair of actions is mutex, so layers and plan steps coincide.
- Trap: Nogoods are goal sets proved unachievable at a layer: a repeat visit is cut immediately instead of searched again. Try example plan-graphplan-nogoods: the goals are non-mutex at P4 but extraction fails at P4 and P5 and succeeds at P6, reusing nogoods.
- Trap: The termination test (graph levelled off and the nogood table at the layer where it levelled stopped growing) proves that no plan exists; it is checked after every failed extraction.

## Partial Order Planning (week 8, Planning)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/plan-pop.html

A planning problem gives an initial state, a goal and operators described in STRIPS form: each operator has preconditions, an add list and a delete list. In the blocks world the operators are pickup, putdown, stack and unstack, and AE means the arm is empty. Partial Order Planning searches the space of plans instead of states, adding steps and orderings only when it must.

Definition: A partial plan has steps, ordering constraints, causal links (A achieves p for B) and open preconditions. Repeatedly support an open precondition with an existing or new step, then resolve threats (a step that deletes p and could fall between A and B) by ordering it before A (demotion) or after B (promotion). Backtrack on failure.

Pseudocode:

```
plan ← {Start, Finish}, Start < Finish, agenda ← goal preconditions of Finish
while agenda not empty
    (p, S) ← pick an open precondition
    choose an achiever A: an existing step that adds p and may precede S, or a new step from the operators
    add causal link A →p→ S and ordering A < S;  if A is new: add A's preconditions to the agenda
    for every step K that deletes p and could fall between A and S (a threat):
        demote (K < A) or promote (S < K), keeping the orderings acyclic
    if no choice works: backtrack
return any linearisation of the steps
```

- threat: K deletes p and possibly A < K < B for link A →p→ B: a step that could undo a protected condition. Ordering K outside the interval keeps every causal link safe, which guarantees the plan works.
- least commitment: order steps only when forced. Avoids the interaction problems that make linear planners fail on the Sussman anomaly.

Finds the optimal 6-step plan for the Sussman anomaly by interleaving subgoals; the search can be expensive.

Complete: yes (with systematic search). Optimal: shortest plan with iterative deepening. Time: exponential in the worst case. Space: O(plan size) per partial plan.

- Trap: Check threats for new links and for new steps.
- Trap: Never order a step before Start or after Finish.
- Trap: The plan-space search is exponential: this studio declines problems with more than 4 blocks. Try example plan-sussman: 6 steps, no goal clobbering, because the subgoal orderings are chosen only when threats force them.

## Means-ends analysis (week 8, Planning)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/plan-mea.html

Means-ends analysis (the idea behind Newell and Simon's General Problem Solver) works from differences. Compare the current state with the goal, choose the most important difference, and find an operator that reduces it. If the operator cannot be applied yet, its preconditions become a new sub-goal, solved by the same procedure. The difference table says which operator removes which kind of difference.

Definition: Difference table for the blocks world: on(x,y) is removed by stack(x,y); ontable(x) by putdown(x); clear(x) by unstack(z,x) for the block z on x; holding(x) by pickup(x) (x on the table) or unstack(x,y); AE by putdown of the held block. Importance: positional differences first, lower blocks of the goal tower before higher ones (a tower is built from the bottom), then clear, then AE, then holding. Sub-goals are solved in the same importance order. Because MEA never protects facts it has already achieved, a later sub-goal can undo an earlier one: on the Sussman anomaly it keeps destroying and re-making the same facts and the loop check stops it.

Pseudocode:

```
MEA(state, goal):
    while goal ⊄ state
        d ← the most important difference (goal fact not in state)
        O ← operator that adds d            // from the difference table
        MEA(state, pre(O))                  // sub-goal: make O applicable
        if O is not applicable: fail
        state ← apply(O, state)
    return
```

- difference = goal − state: goal facts not currently true. These are exactly what remains to be achieved.

It is the first goal-directed planner: instead of blind search it only considers operators relevant to a difference. Its failure on interacting goals motivates goal protection, partial-order planning and Graphplan.

Complete: no. Optimal: no. Time: depends on the differences. Space: depth of sub-goaling.

- Trap: MEA is not complete: it does not protect earlier achievements, so it can undo its own work and cycle (the Sussman anomaly). Run example plan-sussman to watch it fail and plan-reverse to watch it succeed.
- Trap: The result depends on the importance ordering and on the difference table; a different table can succeed where this one fails.
- Trap: A sub-goal may clobber a fact achieved earlier: after each operator, recompute all differences.

## AO* (week 9, Problem decomposition)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/andor-ao-star.html

Some problems split into subproblems that must all be solved (AND), while others offer alternative ways to proceed (OR). AO* searches such AND–OR graphs for the cheapest solution graph, revising its choices as costs become known.

Definition: Each node has connectors: a single-child connector is an OR option, a multi-child connector is an AND arc. Cost of a connector = its arc costs + sum of its children's costs. A node's cost is its cheapest connector, which is marked. AO* expands an unexpanded node on the marked partial solution, then revises costs and markings upwards.

Pseudocode:

```
repeat until start is SOLVED (or its cost exceeds FUTILITY)
    trace marked connectors from start; pick an unexpanded node n on that partial solution
    expand n: add its connectors and children (cost h); no connectors → cost FUTILITY
    S ← {n}
    while S not empty
        take m from S that has no descendant in S
        for each connector c of m: cost(c) = k(c) + Σ cost(children of c)
        cost(m) ← min over c;  mark the best connector
        if every child of the marked connector is SOLVED: label m SOLVED
        if cost(m) changed or m became SOLVED: add m's parents to S
```

- cost(c) = Σ over children t of (k + cost(t)): every arc of a connector costs k, plus its children. An AND arc needs all its children, so their costs add.
- cost(n) = min over connectors c of n of cost(c): choose the cheapest way to solve n. OR alternatives: only the best one is needed.

With admissible estimates AO* finds an optimal solution graph. The marked solution can change as estimates are corrected, which is visible in the trace.

Complete: yes. Optimal: yes with admissible h. Time: exponential in general. Space: the explicit graph.

- Trap: An AND connector costs the sum, not the minimum, of its children.
- Trap: Propagate revisions to all ancestors whose marked connector uses the node. Try example andor-revision: the marked connector of A changes twice.
- Trap: A node with no connectors that is not solved is a dead end: its cost is FUTILITY, and every connector using it must be revised (example andor-futility: A abandons B for the AND connector C+D).

## Backward chaining (goal tree) (week 9, Problem decomposition)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/rules-backward-chaining.html

Forward chaining starts from the facts and derives everything it can. Backward chaining starts from a query (the goal) and works the other way: which rule could conclude this, and what would I then have to show? Only rules relevant to the goal are ever examined, which is why it suits diagnosis and question answering.

Definition: To prove a goal G: (1) if some fact unifies with G, G is solved; (2) otherwise, for each rule whose THEN part unifies with G, make each IF condition a sub-goal. The conditions of one rule form an AND connector (all must be proved); the different rules that could conclude G are OR alternatives. Variables are bound by unification and the bindings are carried from one condition to the next. This is the same AND–OR structure as in problem decomposition.

Pseudocode:

```
Prove(goal, bindings):
    for each fact f that unifies with goal: succeed (f is a solved leaf)
    for each rule R whose consequent unifies with goal:        # OR over rules
        prove every condition of R in turn, carrying the bindings   # AND over conditions
        if all succeed: goal is proved by R
    if nothing works: goal fails (backtrack to the last choice)
    (a goal identical to one of its own ancestors fails: it would loop)
```

- solved(G) = fact(G) ∨ ⋁ over rules R concluding G of ⋀ solved(c), c in IF(R): a goal is solved by a fact, or by some rule all of whose conditions are solved. OR across the alternative rules and AND across the conditions of one rule is exactly an AND–OR graph.

Every goal it proves is also derived by forward chaining (both are sound), but it only does the work needed for the query. An ancestor check is needed because rule bases can be recursive.

Complete: no for recursive rule bases (depth-first), yes on acyclic ones. Optimal: n/a. Time: exponential in the worst case. Space: the goal tree (depth × branching).

- Trap: The first matching fact or rule is not always the right one: bindings may make a later condition fail, and then it must backtrack. Try example rules-backtrack: rule F1 fails on (heavy tweety), the grey branch is undone, and F2 proves the goal.
