- Trap: Rule variables are renamed apart for each use, so ?x in two different uses are different variables.
- Trap: Without the ancestor check a recursive rule (ancestor defined through ancestor) can loop forever.
- Trap: This stepper proves the first answer found; a query with variables may have several answers.

## Forward chaining (week 10, Rule-based systems)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/rules-forward-chaining.html

A rule-based system holds facts in working memory and knowledge as if–then rules. Forward chaining starts from the facts and keeps firing rules whose conditions match until nothing new can be derived.

Definition: The recognise–act cycle: match all rules against working memory to form the conflict set of rule instantiations; resolve the conflict by choosing one (rule order, recency, specificity); execute its actions; repeat. A fired instantiation is not fired again (refractoriness).

Pseudocode:

```
repeat
    MATCH:   conflict set ← every (rule, bindings) whose conditions hold in WM and that has not fired
    if the conflict set is empty: stop
    RESOLVE: pick one by the strategy (rule order, recency or specificity)
    EXECUTE: apply its actions to WM (add / remove facts); remember it fired (refractoriness)
```

- instantiation = (rule, variable bindings): a rule with its ?variables filled in consistently. The same rule can fire several times with different bindings.

Data-driven reasoning, natural for monitoring and configuration. Naive matching repeats work each cycle; Rete removes that cost.

Complete: derives every consequence (add-only rules). Optimal: n/a. Time: match cost per cycle. Space: WM + conflict set.

- Trap: A variable must bind to the same value in every condition of a rule.
- Trap: Conflict resolution changes the order, not the final set of derived facts (for rules that only add). Try example rules-conflict with the three strategies: the first firing is R1 ann, R1 bob or R2 ann.
- Trap: With remove actions or NOT conditions the strategy can change the final facts, because firing one rule can destroy the match of another.

## Rete algorithm (week 10, Rule-based systems)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/rules-rete.html

Most cycles of a rule system change only a few facts, yet naive matching re-checks every rule against everything. The Rete algorithm compiles the rules into a network that remembers partial matches, so each new fact is matched only where it matters.

Definition: Alpha nodes test single patterns and store matching facts. Beta (join) nodes combine a stored partial match (token) from the left with a fact from the right when their variable bindings agree, and pass the result on. A negative (NOT) node passes a token on only while no fact matches the negated pattern with consistent bindings; when such a fact arrives later it blocks the token and withdraws everything built from it, and when that fact is removed the token is released again. Terminal nodes add complete matches to the conflict set. Rules that share leading patterns share nodes.

Pseudocode:

```
compile: one alpha memory per distinct pattern;
         for each rule a chain of join nodes (shared when rules start with the same patterns) ending in a terminal
add fact w:
    for each alpha memory whose pattern matches w: store w, then
        right-activate its join nodes: combine w with each token in the left memory whose bindings agree
        each new token goes to the next join node, or to the terminal → add the instantiation to the conflict set
fire instantiations (rule order); each new fact is added the same way
```

- work per new fact ∝ affected tokens, not |rules| × |WM|: incremental matching. Stored partial matches mean old facts are never matched again.

Trades memory (all partial matches) for speed, which made large production systems practical.

Complete: same matches as naive matching. Optimal: n/a. Time: proportional to change. Space: all partial matches.

- Trap: Joins compare bindings of shared variables only.
- Trap: Node sharing comes from identical condition prefixes.
- Trap: A negated condition makes the system non-monotonic: a match can enter the conflict set and later be withdrawn when a blocking fact arrives. Try example rules-negation: R2 opus is withdrawn after R1 adds (penguin opus).
- Trap: Rete returns the same facts as forward chaining, including with NOT conditions and remove actions; here it fires by rule order, then recency.

## Backtracking (week 11, Constraint processing)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/csp-backtracking.html

A constraint satisfaction problem has variables, each with a domain of values, and constraints saying which combinations are allowed. A solution assigns every variable a value from its domain so that every constraint holds. Backtracking is depth-first search over partial assignments.

Definition: Assign variables in a fixed order. Try each value; keep it if it is consistent with the earlier assignments and continue; if no value works, return to the previous variable and try its next value.

Pseudocode:

```
Backtrack(assignment, i):
    if i > n: return assignment
    for each value a in D(Xᵢ)
        if a is consistent with every assigned neighbour of Xᵢ
            result ← Backtrack(assignment + {Xᵢ = a}, i + 1)
            if result ≠ failure: return result
    return failure                          # go back to Xᵢ₋₁
```

- search tree size ≤ d + d² + … + dⁿ: up to dⁿ complete assignments. Each level multiplies the branches by the domain size.

Complete and simple, but it discovers failures late (thrashing). Look-ahead (forward checking) and consistency (arc consistency) detect them earlier.

Complete: yes. Optimal: n/a (any solution). Time: O(dⁿ) worst case. Space: O(n).

- Trap: Count every value tried as a node.
- Trap: Thrashing: backtracking returns to the most recent variable, even if it is not the cause of the failure, and so it rediscovers the same dead end under every combination of irrelevant earlier values. Try example 'Thrashing': 45 values tried where forward checking needs 6.
- Trap: The variable order changes the tree a lot, and a bad order is only found out by running it. Try example 'Variable ordering': 58 values in the given order, 7 with 'most constraints first'. It is a heuristic, not a guarantee: on the Australia map the given order is better (11 vs 15 values).
- Trap: Backtracking only checks a value against EARLIER variables, so a conflict with a later variable is found only when that variable is reached. Forward checking moves that test forward.

## Forward checking (week 11, Constraint processing)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/csp-forward-checking.html

A constraint satisfaction problem has variables, each with a domain of values, and constraints saying which combinations are allowed. A solution assigns every variable a value from its domain so that every constraint holds. Forward checking combines search with a little reasoning: it looks ahead after each assignment.

Definition: After assigning X = a, remove from the domains of X's unassigned neighbours every value that conflicts with a. If a domain becomes empty, reject a immediately.

Pseudocode:

```
FC(assignment, domains, i):
    if i > n: return assignment
    for each value a in D(Xᵢ)
        D' ← copy of domains;  D'(Xᵢ) ← {a}
        for each unassigned neighbour Y: remove from D'(Y) values inconsistent with Xᵢ = a
        if no D'(Y) is empty: result ← FC(assignment + {Xᵢ = a}, D', i + 1); if result: return it
    return failure
```

- D(Y) ← { b ∈ D(Y) : (a, b) allowed by C(X,Y) }: keep only values compatible with the new assignment. Any value removed could never be part of a solution extending X = a.

Usually far fewer nodes than plain backtracking; pairs well with choosing the variable with the smallest remaining domain (MRV).

Complete: yes. Optimal: n/a. Time: O(dⁿ) worst case. Space: O(n·d) for domain copies.

- Trap: Forward checking does not check two future variables against each other; arc consistency does. Try example 'G = W wipes out E': forward checking accepts G = W and only fails two assignments later.
- Trap: It only pays off together with a good variable order. Smallest domain first (MRV) picks the variable most likely to fail next (the 'fail-first' principle); see example 'Variable ordering' (27 values in the given order, 6 with MRV).
- Trap: Forward checking removes the thrashing of plain backtracking on example 'Thrashing': 6 values against 45, because A = r empties D(E) at once, but it spends extra work at every node pruning domains.

## Arc consistency (AC-1, AC-3) (week 11, Constraint processing)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/csp-ac3.html

A constraint satisfaction problem has variables, each with a domain of values, and constraints saying which combinations are allowed. A solution assigns every variable a value from its domain so that every constraint holds. Arc consistency removes values that cannot possibly be part of any solution, before or during search.

Definition: An arc (X, Y) is consistent if every value of X has some supporting value in Y. Revise(X, Y) deletes unsupported values. AC-1 revises every arc until a whole pass changes nothing; AC-3 keeps a queue and re-examines only arcs pointing into a variable whose domain just shrank.

Pseudocode:

```
Revise(X, Y):
    for each a in D(X): if no b in D(Y) satisfies the constraint: delete a from D(X)
    return whether D(X) changed

AC-3:
    Q ← every arc (X, Y)
    while Q not empty
        (X, Y) ← pop(Q)
        if Revise(X, Y): add every arc (Z, X) with Z ≠ Y to Q
AC-1: repeat Revise on all arcs until a full pass changes nothing
```

- a ∈ D(X) survives ⇔ ∃ b ∈ D(Y): (a, b) ∈ C(X, Y): a value needs a partner on every arc. A value with no partner can never satisfy that constraint, so it can be deleted safely.
- AC-3: O(e · d³): each arc is re-queued at most d times, each revision costs d². Domains only shrink, so the work is bounded.

Cheap reasoning that shrinks domains; sometimes it solves the problem outright (the chain example), sometimes it only prunes (map colouring).

Complete: no (filtering only). Optimal: n/a. Time: O(e·d³) for AC-3 (AC-1: O(n·e·d³)). Space: O(e).

- Trap: Arcs are directed: (X, Y) and (Y, X) are different.
- Trap: Arc consistency does not guarantee a solution exists, nor that it finds one. Three outcomes to compare: 'Ordering chain' is solved by AC-3 alone (every domain becomes one value); 'Variable ordering' is pruned (D = 1, E = 2) but A, B, C stay ambiguous so search is needed; on the Australia map nothing is deleted at all. The 'Two colours on a triangle' example passes arc consistency yet has no solution: only path consistency sees it.
- Trap: AC-1 and AC-3 delete exactly the same values; AC-3 only does less work (fewer revisions), which you can see in the revisions counter by switching the algorithm.

## Path consistency (PC, i-consistency) (week 11, Constraint processing)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/csp-path-consistency.html

Arc consistency looks at one constraint at a time. Path consistency looks at a path of two constraints through a third variable, which is the smallest way to notice that constraints interact.

Definition: The network is i-consistent if every consistent assignment to any i − 1 variables can be extended to any i-th variable. Arc consistency is 2-consistency; path consistency is 3-consistency: every consistent pair (X = a, Y = b) can be extended to every third variable Z. Enforcing it deletes pairs from the relation R(X,Y), possibly making a new implicit constraint between variables that had none.

Pseudocode:

```
PC-1:
    R(X,Y) ← allowed pairs of the constraint, or all pairs if X and Y are unconstrained
    repeat
        for each triangle (X, Z, Y)
            R(X,Y) ← R(X,Y) ∩ ( R(X,Z) ∘ R(Z,Y) )       # (a,b) needs a witness c in D(Z)
    until no relation changed
    if some R(X,Y) is empty: no solution
```

- R(X,Y) ← R(X,Y) ∩ { (a,b) : ∃ c ∈ D(Z), (a,c) ∈ R(X,Z) ∧ (c,b) ∈ R(Z,Y) }: keep a pair only if the third variable can be given a value that works with both. In any solution containing X = a, Y = b, the variable Z has some value c, and that value must satisfy both constraints, so pairs with no such c cannot be in a solution.
- k-consistency: every consistent (k−1)-assignment extends to any k-th variable: k = 1 node, k = 2 arc, k = 3 path. Higher k reasons about bigger groups, at a higher cost; k = n gives a backtrack-free search.

Two colours on a triangle: each value has a partner on every edge, so arc consistency removes nothing, yet three mutually different variables with two values cannot exist. Path consistency empties a relation and proves it.

Complete: no (filtering only). Optimal: n/a. Time: O(n³·d³) per sweep. Space: O(n²·d²).

- Trap: Try example 'Two colours on a triangle': run Arc consistency first (nothing is deleted), then this algorithm (a relation becomes empty). Path consistency is strictly stronger than arc consistency, and also costlier.
- Trap: Path consistency prunes PAIRS (it changes constraints), not just values; domains shrink only afterwards, when arc consistency is run on the tightened relations (done in the last step).
- Trap: It can add constraints between variables that had none: unconstrained pairs start as 'all pairs allowed'.
- Trap: The i-consistency hierarchy (strong i-consistency for i = n gives backtrack-free search) is shown as background; only the 3-consistency algorithm is traced. The remark on strong k-consistency is **supplementary**.

## Waltz algorithm (week 11, Constraint processing)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/csp-waltz.html

How do we see 3D shapes in a line drawing? Waltz showed that each junction of lines allows only a few physical interpretations, and that neighbouring junctions must agree. Propagating that agreement usually leaves a single interpretation.

Definition: Lines get labels: + (convex edge), − (concave edge) or an arrow (occluding boundary, object on the right). Each junction type (L, fork, arrow, T) has a catalogue of allowed labellings (6, 5, 3, 4: the Huffman–Clowes catalogue). Waltz filtering is arc consistency between junctions that share a line.

Pseudocode:

```
for each junction J: D(J) ← catalogue labellings for J's type (L 6, fork 5, arrow 3, T 4)
if the background is known: keep only labellings with outer lines as arrows (object on the right)
Q ← every pair of junctions sharing a line
while Q not empty
    (J, K) ← pop(Q)
    delete from D(J) every labelling whose label on line J–K no labelling in D(K) agrees with
    if D(J) shrank: push (I, J) for every other neighbour I of J
labels agree: + with +, − with −, an arrow leaving J with the same arrow entering K
```

- 18 junction labellings: L 6, fork 5, arrow 3, T 4: the Huffman–Clowes catalogue for trihedral scenes. Only these arise from corners where three planes meet, viewed generically.
- agree(+,+), agree(−,−), agree(→ leaving J, → entering K): a line has one label seen from both ends. This is the binary constraint propagated between junctions.

Constraint propagation instead of search: the cube drawing becomes unambiguous once the background is fixed. Without that, several interpretations survive.

Complete: filtering only. Optimal: n/a. Time: linear for planar drawings. Space: O(junctions).

- Trap: Arrow labels are relative to direction: 'out' at one end is 'in' at the other.
- Trap: Arc consistency can leave several labellings; a search step picks among them. Compare the two cube examples: with the background constraint every junction ends with one labelling; without it junction O keeps one but P to U keep 2 or 3 each (several 3-D readings of the same drawing survive).
- Trap: Waltz filtering is only as good as the catalogue: it assumes trihedral vertices in general position, so drawings of other objects can be labelled wrongly or not at all.

## Model-based diagnosis (week 11, Constraint processing)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/csp-diagnosis.html

When a device misbehaves, model-based diagnosis asks: which components, if broken, would explain what we observe? It uses models of how each component should behave and looks for contradictions.

Definition: Assume a set of components works and propagate values through their models. A contradiction with an observation means that set cannot all be working: it is a conflict set. A diagnosis is a minimal set of components that intersects every minimal conflict.

Pseudocode:

```
for each set S of components assumed OK
    propagate values using only the models of S (forward and backward through + and ×)
    if some wire gets two different values: S is inconsistent
conflicts ← minimal inconsistent sets
diagnoses ← minimal sets of components that intersect every conflict (minimal hitting sets)
```

- diagnosis D: D ∩ C ≠ ∅ for every conflict C, D minimal: blame at least one component in every conflict. If any conflict had no faulty member, the contradiction would remain.

The polybox has conflicts {M1, M2, A1} and {M1, M3, A1, A2}, giving the diagnoses {M1}, {A1} (single faults, they sit in both conflicts) and {M2, M3}, {M2, A2} (double faults). Which diagnoses exist depends on the symptoms: in example 'both outputs wrong' the conflicts are {M1, M2, A1} and {M2, M3, A2} and the single fault {M2} explains both.

Complete: yes (all minimal diagnoses). Optimal: n/a. Time: exponential in components (direct form). Space: O(conflicts).

- Trap: A conflict lists the components used to derive the contradiction, not just the one producing the wrong output.
- Trap: Diagnoses are minimal: supersets also explain the symptoms but are less likely.
- Trap: A component in only some of the conflicts cannot be a single fault: M2 is not enough on the Polybox example (it is not in the second conflict) but is enough on 'both outputs wrong'.
- Trap: If the observations agree with the model there is no conflict and the only minimal diagnosis is the empty set: nothing is faulty.

## SAT as a CSP: backtracking with unit propagation (DPLL) (week 11, SAT · constraint processing)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/sat-dpll.html

The local-search methods of weeks 3 and 4 move between complete assignments and can only find solutions. Constraint processing instead builds an assignment variable by variable, so a dead end is detected as soon as one clause becomes impossible, and the search is complete: if no solution exists it says so. This page is the Davis–Putnam–Logemann–Loveland style of backtracking on a CNF formula, viewed as a CSP whose variables have the domain {T, F}.

Definition: A clause is satisfied once some literal is true and empty (a conflict) once all its literals are false. A unit clause has exactly one unassigned literal and none true, so that literal must be true. A pure literal occurs with only one sign in the clauses not yet satisfied, so making it true cannot hurt. Backtrack on an empty clause; otherwise branch on the first unassigned variable (alphabetical order, as in the course), trying T before F.

Pseudocode:

```
DPLL(assignment):
    repeat
        if some clause has every literal false: return FAIL          # empty clause
        if every clause is satisfied: return assignment
        if a clause has exactly one unassigned literal and no true literal: assign it true    # unit propagation
        else if a variable occurs with one polarity only in the open clauses: assign it so    # pure literal
        else break
    X ← first unassigned variable
    for each value v in {T, F}
        result ← DPLL(assignment + {X = v})
        if result ≠ FAIL: return result
        undo X = v and everything it forced
    return FAIL
```

- unit: |{ℓ ∈ C : ℓ unassigned}| = 1 and no ℓ ∈ C true: one open literal left in an unsatisfied clause. The clause is false unless that literal is true, so setting it is forced, not a choice, and costs no branching.
- empty: every ℓ ∈ C false: the conflict test. A clause is a disjunction; if all its literals are false the clause is false, and assignments only ever add more false literals deeper in the tree.
- leaves ≤ 2^(number of decisions): propagation shrinks the tree. Only decisions branch; forced assignments follow without a choice, so the more propagation, the fewer decisions on any path.

Where hill climbing from 0000 stops at 1000 (h 5), backtracking cannot be fooled by a local maximum: it either reaches an assignment satisfying every clause or has tried all possibilities. Related CSP pages: Backtracking (csp-backtracking) is the plain version of this search, Forward checking (csp-forward-checking) is what unit propagation does after each assignment, and Arc consistency (csp-ac3) generalises it by propagating until nothing more can be removed.

Complete: yes. Optimal: n/a (any satisfying assignment). Time: O(2ⁿ) worst case. Space: O(n) depth.

- Trap: See the pieces separately on the example sat-implication-chain: clauses 1–3 give a chain of unit propagations (a, b, c) with no decision, g is a pure literal, the decision d = T runs into an empty clause (backtrack) and d = F succeeds. Value order F first removes the backtrack; pure literal 'No' makes g a unit propagation instead. sat-unsat shows the UNSAT proof: every branch ends in an empty clause.
- Trap: A conflict means undo to the last decision; forced assignments are not retried with the other value.
- Trap: Unassigned variables at the end are free, not False: the printed bit string fills them with 0 only for display.
- Trap: Pure literals and unit propagation never lose solutions, but without them the same formula needs more backtracks.
- Trap: An 'UNSAT' answer is a proof (all branches closed), whereas local search failing to find a solution proves nothing.

## Partial look-ahead (week 12, Constraint processing · lookahead)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/csp-lookahead-partial.html

Look-ahead methods reason about the future variables after every assignment, so that dead ends are found one or more levels earlier. Forward checking only compares the variable just assigned with its future neighbours; the look-ahead methods also compare the future variables with each other.

Definition: After assigning Xᵢ = a: (1) forward checking, then (2) forward checking, then each future variable Xᵢ is also revised against the LATER future variables Xⱼ (j > i) in one pass. If any future domain becomes empty, reject a at once. This is the "Partial look-ahead" variant: one pass, arcs (Xᵢ, Xⱼ) with i before j.

Pseudocode:

```
Lookahead(assignment, domains, i):          # mode = partial
    if i > n: return assignment
    for each value a in D(Xᵢ)
        D' ← copy of domains;  D'(Xᵢ) ← {a}
        forward check: prune D'(Y) of every unassigned neighbour Y against Xᵢ = a
        extra look-ahead (one pass, arcs (Xᵢ, Xⱼ) with i before j):
            revise the future variables against each other
        if no D'(Y) is empty: result ← Lookahead(assignment + {Xᵢ = a}, D', i + 1); if result: return it
    return failure
```

- D(Y) ← { b ∈ D(Y) : ∃ c ∈ D(Z), (b, c) allowed by C(Y,Z) }: delete values of a future variable Y that have no support in another future variable Z. A value without support can never be part of a solution extending the current assignment, so deleting it is safe.

A future variable can be squeezed empty by two OTHER future variables. Forward checking cannot see that until one of them is assigned; look-ahead sees it now. Example: after G = W the neighbours of G lose W and become single-valued, which empties D(E); only the look-ahead variants notice (see the example 'G = W wipes out E').

Complete: yes. Optimal: n/a. Time: O(dⁿ) worst case, smaller tree than forward checking. Space: O(n·d) for domain copies.

- Trap: The three variants prune in a strict order: forward checking < partial < full < MAC (each prunes at least what the previous one does). Example 'Look-ahead ladder' shows 17, 6, 5 and 3 values tried before the same conclusion (no solution).
- Trap: Partial look-ahead depends on the variable order: a variable that is last in the ordering is never revised against anything, so it may miss a wipe-out that full look-ahead finds.
- Trap: More pruning per node does not always mean less total time; each node costs more.
- Trap: Which pruning came from forward checking and which from the extra look-ahead is shown in separate columns. The split into 'partial / full / MAC' passes is the usual textbook presentation; the exact pass structure is **supplementary** to the lecture slides.

## Full look-ahead (week 12, Constraint processing · lookahead)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/csp-lookahead-full.html

Look-ahead methods reason about the future variables after every assignment, so that dead ends are found one or more levels earlier. Forward checking only compares the variable just assigned with its future neighbours; the look-ahead methods also compare the future variables with each other.

Definition: After assigning Xᵢ = a: (1) forward checking, then (2) forward checking, then every arc between two future variables is revised once, in both directions. If any future domain becomes empty, reject a at once. This is the "Full look-ahead" variant: one pass over all future arcs.

Pseudocode:

```
Lookahead(assignment, domains, i):          # mode = full
    if i > n: return assignment
    for each value a in D(Xᵢ)
        D' ← copy of domains;  D'(Xᵢ) ← {a}
        forward check: prune D'(Y) of every unassigned neighbour Y against Xᵢ = a
        extra look-ahead (one pass over all future arcs):
            revise the future variables against each other
        if no D'(Y) is empty: result ← Lookahead(assignment + {Xᵢ = a}, D', i + 1); if result: return it
    return failure
```

- D(Y) ← { b ∈ D(Y) : ∃ c ∈ D(Z), (b, c) allowed by C(Y,Z) }: delete values of a future variable Y that have no support in another future variable Z. A value without support can never be part of a solution extending the current assignment, so deleting it is safe.

A future variable can be squeezed empty by two OTHER future variables. Forward checking cannot see that until one of them is assigned; look-ahead sees it now. Example: after G = W the neighbours of G lose W and become single-valued, which empties D(E); only the look-ahead variants notice (see the example 'G = W wipes out E').

Complete: yes. Optimal: n/a. Time: O(dⁿ) worst case, smaller tree than forward checking. Space: O(n·d) for domain copies.

- Trap: The three variants prune in a strict order: forward checking < partial < full < MAC (each prunes at least what the previous one does). Example 'Look-ahead ladder' shows 17, 6, 5 and 3 values tried before the same conclusion (no solution).
- Trap: Partial look-ahead depends on the variable order: a variable that is last in the ordering is never revised against anything, so it may miss a wipe-out that full look-ahead finds.
- Trap: More pruning per node does not always mean less total time; each node costs more.
- Trap: Which pruning came from forward checking and which from the extra look-ahead is shown in separate columns. The split into 'partial / full / MAC' passes is the usual textbook presentation; the exact pass structure is **supplementary** to the lecture slides.

## Arc-consistency look-ahead (MAC) (week 12, Constraint processing · lookahead)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/csp-lookahead-mac.html

Look-ahead methods reason about the future variables after every assignment, so that dead ends are found one or more levels earlier. Forward checking only compares the variable just assigned with its future neighbours; the look-ahead methods also compare the future variables with each other.

Definition: After assigning Xᵢ = a: (1) forward checking, then (2) forward checking, then AC-3 on the future variables until nothing changes (maintaining arc consistency). If any future domain becomes empty, reject a at once. This is the "Arc-consistency look-ahead (MAC)" variant: AC-3 to a fixpoint.

Pseudocode:

```
Lookahead(assignment, domains, i):          # mode = mac
    if i > n: return assignment
    for each value a in D(Xᵢ)
        D' ← copy of domains;  D'(Xᵢ) ← {a}
        forward check: prune D'(Y) of every unassigned neighbour Y against Xᵢ = a
        extra look-ahead (AC-3 to a fixpoint):
            revise the future variables against each other
        if no D'(Y) is empty: result ← Lookahead(assignment + {Xᵢ = a}, D', i + 1); if result: return it
    return failure
```

- D(Y) ← { b ∈ D(Y) : ∃ c ∈ D(Z), (b, c) allowed by C(Y,Z) }: delete values of a future variable Y that have no support in another future variable Z. A value without support can never be part of a solution extending the current assignment, so deleting it is safe.

A future variable can be squeezed empty by two OTHER future variables. Forward checking cannot see that until one of them is assigned; look-ahead sees it now. Example: after G = W the neighbours of G lose W and become single-valued, which empties D(E); only the look-ahead variants notice (see the example 'G = W wipes out E').

Complete: yes. Optimal: n/a. Time: O(dⁿ) worst case, smaller tree than forward checking. Space: O(n·d) for domain copies.

- Trap: The three variants prune in a strict order: forward checking < partial < full < MAC (each prunes at least what the previous one does). Example 'Look-ahead ladder' shows 17, 6, 5 and 3 values tried before the same conclusion (no solution).
- Trap: Partial look-ahead depends on the variable order: a variable that is last in the ordering is never revised against anything, so it may miss a wipe-out that full look-ahead finds.
- Trap: More pruning per node does not always mean less total time; each node costs more.
- Trap: Which pruning came from forward checking and which from the extra look-ahead is shown in separate columns. The split into 'partial / full / MAC' passes is the usual textbook presentation; the exact pass structure is **supplementary** to the lecture slides.

## Conflict-directed backjumping (week 12, Constraint processing · lookback)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/csp-cbj.html

Chronological backtracking returns to the previous variable even when that variable has nothing to do with the failure. Conflict-directed backjumping is a look-back method: it analyses the failure and jumps back to the variable that is actually responsible.

Definition: Each variable Xᵢ carries a conflict set conf(Xᵢ): the earlier variables whose current values rejected some value of Xᵢ. When Xᵢ has no value left, jump to the deepest variable h in conf(Xᵢ), unassign everything in between, merge conf(Xᵢ) − {h} into conf(h), and let h try its next value.

Pseudocode:

```
CBJ(i):                                  # variables X₁…Xₙ in a fixed order
    conf(Xᵢ) ← { }
    for each value a in D(Xᵢ)
        if a clashes with an assigned Xⱼ (j < i): add Xⱼ to conf(Xᵢ); try next value
        else assign Xᵢ = a; r ← CBJ(i + 1); if r = success: return success
             if r jumps to h < i: unassign Xᵢ; return r        # Xᵢ is skipped
    h ← deepest variable in conf(Xᵢ)         # no value left
    conf(h) ← conf(h) ∪ conf(Xᵢ) − {h}
    return jump to h
```

- h = max { j : Xⱼ ∈ conf(Xᵢ) }: the jump target is the latest culprit. Every value of Xᵢ clashes with something in conf(Xᵢ); changing a variable outside it cannot help, and the latest culprit is the nearest place where a change might help.
- conf(h) ← conf(h) ∪ conf(Xᵢ) − {h}: pass the blame on. If h fails after its other values are tried, the earlier culprits of Xᵢ are also culprits for h.

Finds exactly the same first solution as chronological backtracking, with the same orders, in fewer or equal nodes: jumping over a variable never skips a solution.

Complete: yes. Optimal: n/a. Time: O(dⁿ) worst case, ≤ backtracking. Space: O(n²) for conflict sets.

- Trap: Try example 'Backjumping' (D fails because of A alone): CBJ jumps from D over B and C to A, 10 values tried against 24 for chronological backtracking. On example 'Thrashing' it needs 16 against 45, but forward checking (6) still beats it: CBJ is look-back, it reacts only after the failure.
- Trap: A jump over a level is only possible when the failing variable has no conflict with the intermediate variables.
- Trap: Conflict sets are only extended by the variables that clashed, not by every earlier variable.
- Trap: The culprit recorded for each value here is the first clashing variable in the ordering (the usual Prosser formulation); other books record all of them. Both are sound; the choice of culprit is **supplementary** to the lecture.

## Depth-First Branch and Bound (week 12, Graph search · optimal)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/search-dfbnb.html

Depth-First Branch and Bound keeps the small memory of depth-first search but still finds the optimal path. It carries a bound U, the cost of the best complete path found so far, and cuts off any branch that already costs at least U.

Definition: Explore depth-first. The first path to the goal sets U = its cost. From then on, a path to node N is pruned when g(N) + h(N) ≥ U, because with an admissible h no completion of it can be cheaper than U. Whenever a cheaper goal path is found, U is lowered. When the search ends, the best path found is optimal. Only the current path is stored, so memory is linear in the depth. With the option 'g only' the heuristic is ignored (h = 0): then the pruning test is g(N) ≥ U.

Pseudocode:

```
U ← ∞;  best ← none
DFBnB(N, g, path):
    if g + h(N) ≥ U: prune; return                 # cannot improve on the best solution
    if GoalTest(N): U ← g;  best ← path;  return   # a better solution
    for each child C of N not on the path, in increasing order of g' + h(C):
        DFBnB(C, g + k(N,C), path + C)
return best
```

- prune N when g(N) + h(N) ≥ U: its best possible total is no better than the bound. With h ≤ h* the true cost of any path through N is at least g(N)+h(N), so continuing cannot help.
- U ← min(U, g(goal)): tighten the bound at each solution. A smaller U prunes more of the remaining tree.

It needs memory only for the current path, unlike A* whose OPEN list can grow exponentially, and it still returns an optimal path. Its weakness is that, on a graph, it may reach the same state again by many paths. A good first solution (found by ordering children well) makes it prune heavily.

Complete: yes (finite graph). Optimal: yes with admissible h. Time: exponential worst case. Space: O(b·d).

- Trap: The first goal found is not the answer: keep searching with the bound.
- Trap: With an inadmissible h the pruning can discard the optimal path; with h = 0 ('g only') it is always safe.
- Trap: A bad child ordering finds a poor U late and prunes little. On the 'Weighted graph' U improves twice (first S–A–C–E–G = 13, then the optimum S–B–E–G = 12) and every later branch is cut by g + h ≥ U.
- Trap: Prune with ≥ U: a path equal to U cannot improve the answer.
- Trap: Unlike A*, the first solution is usually not optimal; the search only stops when every branch is pruned. Use 'g only' to see the bound work without a heuristic: more branches survive.

## Nogood recording (week 12, Constraint processing · lookback)

URL: https://1mystic.github.io/SearchStudio/learn/csp-nogood.html

Backtracking can discover the same dead end again and again under different irrelevant assignments. Nogood recording is a look-back method that remembers a dead end in a general form so it is never rediscovered.

Definition: A nogood is a partial assignment that cannot be extended to a solution. When Xᵢ has no value left, the values of the variables in its conflict set form a nogood. Later, any assignment that contains a stored nogood is rejected immediately.

Pseudocode:

```
Nogood-BT(i):
    conf(Xᵢ) ← { }
    for each value a in D(Xᵢ)
        if some stored nogood ⊆ assignment + {Xᵢ = a}: add its other variables to conf(Xᵢ); skip a   # pruned by a nogood
        else if a clashes with an assigned Xⱼ: add Xⱼ to conf(Xᵢ); skip a
        else assign Xᵢ = a; if Nogood-BT(i + 1) succeeds: return success
             else add the failed child's conflict set − {Xᵢ} to conf(Xᵢ)
    store nogood { Xⱼ = value(Xⱼ) : Xⱼ ∈ conf(Xᵢ) }         # unless a smaller stored nogood already covers it
    return failure                                            # chronological: go back to Xᵢ₋₁
```

- nogood = { Xⱼ = vⱼ : Xⱼ ∈ conf(Xᵢ) }: the culprits and their current values. The values in conf(Xᵢ) alone already exclude every value of Xᵢ, so any assignment containing them is hopeless, whatever else it says.

Small nogoods prune big parts of the tree. In the example 'Nogood recording' the single nogood {A=r} found at D rejects three later values (C=z, B=y, B=z) without any search.

Complete: yes. Optimal: n/a. Time: O(dⁿ) worst case, ≤ backtracking. Space: O(number of nogoods).

- Trap: Try example 'Nogood recording': the dead end at D is stored as {A=r} and later rejects C=z, B=y and B=z without search (10 nodes against 24 for plain backtracking). Nogood recording is chronological, so it still goes back one level at a time; CBJ jumps but forgets, nogoods remember but do not jump.
- Trap: A nogood only prunes assignments that contain ALL of its variable-value pairs.
- Trap: Storing every nogood costs memory; real systems bound the size or the number of nogoods.
- Trap: Nogoods whose variables are already covered by a smaller stored nogood are not stored again. This subsumption test is **supplementary**.
